label: lem:smash
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Zero smash products

title: Proof
body_md:
A zero coordinate stays zero after multiplication on either
side or addition of any tuple.  Hence $J$ is a two-sided
multiplicative ideal and absorbs addition; its Rees relation
is a congruence.  For a surviving tuple, collect its left
indices, group labels, and right indices into three tuples.
A product survives exactly when every pair of corresponding
middle indices agrees.  Two distinct surviving tuples differ
in some coordinate, so their sum has a zero coordinate and
collapses.  These facts prove both operations in
\eqref{eq:smash}, without a finiteness assumption.
head: environment

label: prop:join
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The two-factor zero smash identifies $B_I(G)$ as a quotient
of $B_I\times \flat(G)$.  Both factors embed
in $B_I(G)$, using identity group labels or one diagonal
corner, proving \eqref{eq:join}.
For finite $I$ with $|I|\geq2$, choose $r$ with
$2^r\geq|I|$.  The zero smash of $r$ copies of
$B_2$ is $B_{2^r}$, which contains
$B_I$.  The reverse inclusion uses two indices.
For infinite $I$, each evaluation of an identity uses only
finitely many indices and lies in a finite-index Brandt
subsemiring.  Thus the same identities hold.  Equation
\eqref{eq:join} gives the assertion for arbitrary $G$.
head: environment

label: thm:orthogonal
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Exact variety of an orthogonal sum

title: Proof
body_md:
The coordinate-axis embedding and the inclusions of the
summands give
\[
 \mathsf{V}(S)=\bigvee_\lambda\mathsf{V}(B_{I_\lambda}(G_\lambda)).
\]
Similarly, by the arbitrary-product zero-smash lemma and
the coordinate subgroup embeddings,
\[
 \bigvee_\lambda\mathsf{V}(\flat(G_\lambda))
   =\mathsf{V}\bigl(\flat(\prod_\lambda G_\lambda)\bigr).
\]
If all index sets are singletons, this is the assertion.
Otherwise $S$ also contains $B_2$, and
Proposition~\ref{prop:join} gives
$B_2(G)\in\mathsf{V}(S)$.
Conversely, every group $G_\lambda$ embeds in
$G$, so every summand belongs to
$\mathsf{V}(B_2(G))$, by index independence.  The
coordinate-axis embedding gives the reverse inclusion.
head: environment

label: lem:constant
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:constant}
Let $S$ be any ai-semiring with an element $0$
absorbing both operations.  It is finitely based in
$\{+,\cdot\}$ if and only if its expansion naming
that zero is finitely based in $\{+,\cdot,0\}$.
The existence of a basis with a uniform finite variable
bound is also equivalent in the two signatures.
No nonzero idempotent hypothesis is needed.
head: environment
name: Conservativity of an absorbing constant

title: Proof
body_md:
Given a binary basis, add
\[
 x+0\approx0,\qquad x0\approx0,\qquad0x\approx0.
\]
Every term containing zero reduces to zero.
If a valid expanded identity has the form $\mathbf{p}\approx0$
with $\mathbf{p}$ constant-free, then the binary identity
$\mathbf{p}+y\approx \mathbf{p}$, with $y$ fresh, is valid in $S$.
It follows from the binary basis, and substituting $0$
for $y$ proves $\mathbf{p}\approx0$.
The remaining identities are already binary or reduce
to $0\approx0$.  This proves the forward implication.

Conversely, let $\Sigma$ be a basis of the expansion;
include the ai-semiring axioms if working relative to
that class.  First suppose a constant-free term is
identically zero in $S$.  Identifying all its variables
gives a unary term $\mathbf{q}(x)$ with that property.
In each member of $\Sigma$, replace every $0$ by
$\mathbf{q}(z)$, with $z$ a fresh variable, and add
\[
 \mathbf{q}(x)\approx \mathbf{q}(y),\qquad \mathbf{q}(x)+y\approx \mathbf{q}(x),\qquad
 \mathbf{q}(x)y\approx \mathbf{q}(x),\qquad y\mathbf{q}(x)\approx \mathbf{q}(x).
\]
All these identities are valid in the binary reduct of
$S$.  In any model they make the value of $\mathbf{q}$
a well-defined common absorbing zero.  Naming this
value gives a model of $\Sigma$, so the binary
model satisfies every identity of $S$.
Thus the displayed construction gives a binary basis.

Now suppose there is no constant-free zero term.
Every valid binary identity of $S$ has the same
variable content on both sides: otherwise an exclusively
occurring variable can be assigned zero, and all other
variables a single variable value $x$, producing a
constant-free unary zero term on the opposite side.
For the same reason a valid expanded identity either
contains no zero constant or contains zero on both sides.
Let $\Sigma_{\rm free}$ be the constant-free members
of $\Sigma$, and let $A$ be any binary model of
$\Sigma_{\rm free}$.  Adjoin a fresh element
$\infty$ absorbing both operations.
Matching variable content ensures that every identity
of $\Sigma_{\rm free}$ remains valid: either all
occurring values lie in $A$, or both sides become
$\infty$.  Name $\infty$ as zero.
Every remaining member of $\Sigma$ is then automatic,
so the expansion satisfies $\Sigma$, and its binary
subalgebra $A$ satisfies all binary identities of $S$.
This proves completeness of $\Sigma_{\rm free}$.

The constructions preserve finiteness.  For a possibly
infinite basis with a uniform variable bound they add
at most one variable, and only a fixed finite family
of auxiliary identities.  This proves the last assertion.
head: environment

label: thm:all-groups
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:all-groups}
For every nontrivial group $G$ and every set $I$ with
$|I|\geq2$, the flat Brandt semiring $B_I(G)$ has no
identity basis with a uniform finite bound on the number of
variables.  In particular it is not finitely based.
This holds in both $\{+,\cdot\}$ and $\{+,\cdot,0\}$.
head: environment

label: thm:uniform
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:uniform}
For every $k\geq1$, put
\[
 m=\max\{2,\lfloor k/4\rfloor+1\}.
\]
There is a finite flat semiring $W_k$ with exactly
$10m+2$ elements such that:
\begin{enumerate}[$(\rm i)$]
\item $W_k\notin\mathcal{B}$;
\item every subsemiring of $W_k$ generated by at most $k$
elements belongs to $\mathsf{V}(B_2(C_r))$ for every integer $r\geq2$,
and also belongs to $\mathsf{V}(B_2(\mathbb{Z}))$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently the same $W_k$ satisfies every identity in at most
$k$ variables of every $B_I(G)$ with $|I|\geq2$ and
$G\ne\{1\}$.
head: environment

label: cor:interval
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:interval}
If a variety $\mathcal W\subseteq\mathcal{B}$ contains $B_2(C_p)$
for some prime $p$, or contains $B_2(\mathbb{Z})$, then
$\mathcal W$ has no finite identity basis.  In fact its
identities have no basis with a uniform finite bound on the
number of variables.
head: environment
name: An interval of nonfinitely based varieties

label: cor:brandt-classification
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:brandt-classification}
For every group $G$ and every set $I$ with $|I|\geq2$,
in either stated language,
\[
 B_I(G)\text{ is finitely based}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G=\{1\}.
\]
head: environment
name: All Brandt index sets

title: Proof
body_md:
The negative direction is Theorem~\ref{thm:all-groups}.
For the positive direction, index independence reduces to
$B_2$, whose finite basis in the binary language
is given by \cite[Theorem 1]{Sh}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:constant} deals with the named zero.
head: environment

label: lem:SH
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:SH}
The operations above make $S_H$ a flat ai-semiring.
Its only nonzero products of three factors are $abc=h$ for
edges $abc\in H$.
Every product of four factors, and every square, is zero.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Linearity makes the multiplication table unambiguous.
A nonzero $(xy)z$ must have intermediate product $q_c$;
hence $x=a,y=b,z=c$ for an edge $abc$, and its value is $h$.
A nonzero $x(yz)$ must have intermediate product $p_a$,
giving exactly the same condition and value.
Conversely an edge gives
$a(bc)=ap_a=h=q_cc=(ab)c$.
This proves associativity and the description of triple products.
The other vanishing assertions follow from the disjoint types.

The multiplication is $0$-cancellative:
\[
 xy=xz\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ y=z,\qquad
 yx=zx\ne0\ \Longrightarrow\ y=z.
\]
For instance, with fixed left factor $a$, two products with
$B$-elements having the same output $q_c$ would give two
edges sharing $a,c$, contrary to linearity.
The output $h$ occurs only with right factor $p_a$.
With fixed left factor $b$, equal nonzero outputs $p_a$
would give two edges sharing $a,b$; a left factor $q_c$
has only one nonzero right multiple.
These exhaust the cases.
The corresponding argument for a fixed right factor uses the pairs
$b,c$ and $a,c$ for edge products.

$0$-cancellation implies distributivity
under flat addition.
If $y\ne z$, the products $xy,xz$ are either different or
both zero, since they cannot equal the same nonzero element.
Thus $xy+xz=0=x(y+z)$.
The case $y=z$ is immediate; right distributivity is proved
in the same way.
head: environment

label: lem:prism-identity
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: The prism identity

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider any evaluation in $B_n(G)$.
If $\mathbf{u}_m=0$, the identity holds because zero absorbs addition.
Otherwise flat addition implies that every retained word in
\eqref{eq:prism-faces} has the same nonzero value
$(s,\delta,t)$.
All variables are nonzero, since there are no isolated
vertices in $H_m$.
Write the value of a variable $x$ as
$(\ell_x,g_x,r_x)$.

The matrix indices of the missing word follow from the retained words.
The retained words
$a_0d_{m-1}c_{m-1}$,
$\bar a_0d_{m-1}\bar c_{m-1}$, and
$\bar a_0b_0\bar c_0$ give
\[
 r_{a_0}=\ell_{d_{m-1}}=r_{\bar a_0}=\ell_{b_0}.
\]
The retained words
$\bar a_0b_0\bar c_0$,
$\bar a_1d_0\bar c_0$, and
$a_1d_0c_0$ give
\[
 r_{b_0}=\ell_{\bar c_0}=r_{d_0}=\ell_{c_0}.
\]
Also $\ell_{a_0}=s$ and $r_{c_0}=t$, using
$V_{m-1}$ and $V_0$.
Thus $\mathbf{w}_0$ is composable and has the required outside indices.

We next determine the group label.
In the next calculation use the same letter for the group label
of its evaluated variable, to keep the notation short.
All lower words are retained, so right cancellation gives
\begin{equation}\label{eq:lower-relations}
 \bar a_i b_i=\bar a_{i+1}d_i
 \qquad\text{for every }i.
\end{equation}
For $i\ne0$, the two upper words are also retained, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:upper-relations}
 a_i b_i=a_{i+1}d_i.
\end{equation}
Put $r_i=a_i\bar a_i^{-1}$.
Equation \eqref{eq:lower-relations} gives
$b_i d_i^{-1}=\bar a_i^{-1}\bar a_{i+1}$.
Together with \eqref{eq:upper-relations}, this yields
$r_i=r_{i+1}$ for $i=1,\ldots,m-1$.
Since indices are modulo $m$, these equalities imply
$r_1=r_2=\cdots=r_{m-1}=r_0$.
Now \eqref{eq:lower-relations} at $i=0$ gives
\[
 a_0b_0
 =r_0\bar a_0b_0
 =r_1\bar a_1d_0
 =a_1d_0.
\]
Multiplying by $c_0$, the retained word $V_0$ shows
$a_0b_0c_0=\delta$.
The missing word therefore has value $(s,\delta,t)$,
proving \eqref{eq:prism-identity}.

In $S_{H_m}$, assign every variable its identically named
letter.  All retained words have value $h$ by
Lemma~\ref{lem:SH}, and the missing word has value zero.
Thus the inequality in \eqref{eq:prism-identity} fails,
since $0\nleq h$ in the additive order.
head: environment

label: lem:prism-cuts
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:prism-cuts}
If $\Gamma=C_r\square K_2$, $r\geq4$, and
$\varnothing\ne X\ne V(\Gamma)$, then
$|\partial_\Gamma X|\geq3$.
Equality holds only when $X$ or its complement is a singleton.
head: environment
name: Small cuts of a prism

label: eq:cut-formula
title: Proof
body_md:
Describe $X$ by its upper and lower index sets $I,J$
in the cycle $C_r$.
Then
\begin{equation}\label{eq:cut-formula}
 |\partial_\Gamma X|
 =|\partial_{C_r}I|+|\partial_{C_r}J|+|I\mathbin{\triangle}J|.
\end{equation}
If both $I,J$ are nonempty proper subsets of the cycle,
each of the first two terms is at least two.
Otherwise, after exchanging layers or taking the complement
of $X$, assume $I=\varnothing$.
The set $J$ is nonempty.
If $J$ is the full cycle, the cut has size $r\geq4$.
Otherwise the size is
$|\partial_{C_r}J|+|J|\geq2+|J|$.
It is at most three precisely when $J$ is a singleton.
Undoing the complement and layer exchange gives the assertion.
head: environment

label: lem:short-support
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:short-support}
Suppose that at least two vertices of $\Gamma$ lie outside
$F$.
The vectors $\rho_v$, $v\in F$, are independent over
$R$.
Every nonzero vector of $W_F$ supported on at most three
coordinates is a nonzero scalar multiple of a single
$\rho_v$, $v\in F$.
In particular $W_F$ contains no nonzero vector supported on
at most two coordinates, and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:triple-test}
 e_a+e_b+e_c\in W_F
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad abc\in F
 \qquad(a\in A\cap E_F,\ b\in B\cap E_F,\ c\in C\cap E_F).
\end{equation}
head: environment
name: Short-support relations

title: Proof
body_md:
Give the bipartition classes of $\Gamma$ signs $+1,-1$,
denoted by $\varepsilon(v)$.
For a combination $z=\sum_{v\in F}\lambda_v\rho_v$, put
\[
 f(v)=
 \begin{cases}\varepsilon(v)\lambda_v,&v\in F,\\
 0,&v\notin F.\end{cases}
\]
On a graph edge $uv$, oriented from the positive to the
negative bipartition class, its coefficient in $z$ is
\[
 \lambda_u+\lambda_v=f(u)-f(v),
\]
where coefficients outside $F$ are read as zero.
Thus $\operatorname{supp} z$ is exactly the set of edges joining vertices
with different $f$-values.
If $z=0$, connectedness makes $f$ constant; since $F$
is proper it has value zero outside $F$, so all coefficients
are zero.  This proves independence.

Now suppose $z\ne0$ and $|\operatorname{supp} z|\leq3$.
Choose a nonzero value $\alpha$ of $f$, and set
$X=f^{-1}(\alpha)$.
This is a nonempty proper set, and
$\partial_{\Gamma}X\subseteq\operatorname{supp} z$.
By \eqref{eq:cut-condition}, $X$ or its complement is a
singleton.
The latter is impossible: at least two vertices outside $F$
have value zero, so both lie outside $X$.
Hence $X=\{v\}$, and its three incident edges constitute
all of $\operatorname{supp} z$.

If another vertex had a nonzero value, its nonzero level set
would similarly be a singleton $\{w\}$, with
$\partial\{w\}=\operatorname{supp} z=\partial\{v\}$.
Distinct vertices of a simple cubic graph cannot have identical
sets of three incident edges: that would require three parallel
edges between them.
Thus $f$ is supported only at $v$, and $z=\lambda_v\rho_v$.

Each $\rho_v$ has support exactly three.
This excludes nonzero support sizes one and two.
For \eqref{eq:triple-test}, the forward implication makes
$e_a+e_b+e_c$ a scalar multiple of one $\rho_v$.
Its support and coefficients force the star $v$ to be $abc$
and the scalar to be $1$.
The reverse implication follows from the definition.
head: environment

label: lem:primitive
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:primitive}
For any nonempty proper $F\subset V(\Gamma)$,
\[
 R^{E_F}/W_F\cong R^d,
 \qquad d=|E_F|-|F|\geq2.
\]
In particular the integer row module is a direct summand.
head: environment
name: A free quotient over every coefficient ring

title: Proof
body_md:
Multiply each row by its bipartition sign.  The result is a
restricted oriented incidence matrix, up to column signs.
Root a spanning tree of $\Gamma$ at a vertex outside $F$.
For each $v\in F$, select the column of its edge to its
parent.  These columns are distinct and belong to $E_F$.
Order the rows and their corresponding columns by increasing
depth.  A selected column has its diagonal entry $\pm1$
and at most one other entry, in an earlier row.  Thus the
square selected matrix is triangular with determinant $\pm1$.
It is invertible over every such $R$.

Let $\pi$ be projection to the selected coordinates.
Its restriction $\pi|_{W_F}$ is an isomorphism onto
$R^F$.  Subtracting the unique row combination with
prescribed selected coordinates gives
\[
 R^{E_F}=W_F\oplus\ker\pi,
 \qquad \ker\pi\cong R^{E_F\setminus J},
\]
where $J$ is the selected column set.  This proves freeness
and the rank formula, without division by nonunits or a
finite search for minors.

Let $t=|F|$, let $e$ count the graph edges internal to $F$,
and put $b=|\partial_{\Gamma}F|$.
Cubicity gives $3t=2e+b$, while $|E_F|=e+b$.
Thus
\begin{equation}\label{eq:module-rank}
 d=|E_F|-|F|=\frac{t+b}{2}\geq2,
\end{equation}
because $t\geq1$ and \eqref{eq:cut-condition} gives
$b\geq3$.
head: environment

label: lem:local-representation
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: Local representation

label: eq:labels
title: Proof
body_md:
Take $R=\mathbb{Z}/r\mathbb{Z}$, $r\geq2$, or $\mathbb{Z}$, and form the additive group
\[
 K=R^{E_F}/W_F.
\]
By Lemma~\ref{lem:primitive}, it is $C_r^d$ or $\mathbb{Z}^d$,
respectively, for $d\geq2$.
Write $[x]$ for the basis class of a hypergraph vertex $x$.
This notation distinguishes quotient classes from the formal
barred letters in \eqref{eq:prism-faces}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:short-support} says that distinct vertices
have distinct classes and
\begin{equation}\label{eq:labels}
 [a]+[b]+[c]=0_K
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad abc\in F.
\end{equation}

In $B_4(K)$, generate a subsemiring $T$ by
\begin{equation}\label{eq:local-gens}
 A_a=(1,[a],2),\qquad B_b=(2,[b],3),\qquad
 C_c=(3,[c],4).
\end{equation}
It contains zero, since $A_a^2=0$.
Every nonzero element of $T$ is the value of
a nonempty multiplicative word in these generators:
flat addition can only retain an element or give zero.
The increasing matrix indices restrict such words to length
at most three and positions
\begin{equation}\label{eq:positions}
 (1,2),\ (2,3),\ (3,4),\ (1,3),\ (2,4),\ (1,4).
\end{equation}
The elements
\begin{equation}\label{eq:PQH}
 H_0=(1,0_K,4),\qquad
 P_a=(2,-[a],4),\qquad Q_c=(1,-[c],3)
\end{equation}
belong to $T$.
Indeed, $F$ has an edge, every vertex of $F$ is incident
with one, and \eqref{eq:labels} gives the required two-letter
and three-letter products.
In particular $H_0$ is a nonzero Brandt element, despite its
identity group label.

Let $T^1$ be $T$ with a formal identity
adjoined for the following divisibility criterion:
\[
 D=\{x\in T:uxv=H_0
        \text{ for some }u,v\in T^1\},\qquad
 I=T\setminus D.
\]
Then $0\in I$, $H_0\notin I$, and $I$ is a two-sided
ideal: if $sx$ or $xs$ divides $H_0$, associativity
makes $x$ divide $H_0$.
Also $I+T\subseteq I$, since adding to an
element of $I$ retains it or gives zero.
Collapsing exactly $I$ is therefore a semiring Rees quotient.

All elements in \eqref{eq:local-gens} and \eqref{eq:PQH}
divide $H_0$, using incident edges.
There are no other surviving elements.
The first three positions in \eqref{eq:positions} contain
only the original generators.
An element in position $(1,3)$ is
$(1,[a]+[b],3)=A_aB_b$.
No nonempty left extension is possible, because no nonzero
element of $T$ ends at index $1$.
Its only possible extension to $H_0$ is multiplication on
the right by some $C_c$.
By \eqref{eq:labels}, this happens precisely for an edge
$abc$, when the element is $Q_c$.
Symmetrically the surviving elements in position $(2,4)$
are exactly the $P_a$.
An element in position $(1,4)$ has no nonempty extension
on either side, so it survives only if it equals $H_0$.

Matrix positions separate all the types.
Within each type distinctness follows from the absence of
a nonzero support-two relation in $W_F$.
The same-symbol bijection from $S_F$ onto $T/I$
has precisely the required products:
$A_aB_b$ and $B_bC_c$ survive exactly for edges, while
\[
 A_aP_{a'}=(1,[a]-[a'],4)
\]
survives exactly when $a=a'$, and $Q_cC_{c'}$ survives
exactly when $c=c'$.
All remaining products are zero by their positions.
Both additions are flat and zero is preserved.  Thus
\[
 S_F\cong T/I.
\]

Finally take $L=C_r$ or $L=\mathbb{Z}$, according to the
coefficient ring.
Lemma~\ref{lem:smash} gives
$B_{2^d}(L^d)\in\mathsf{V}(B_2(L))$.
As $d\geq2$ and $K\cong L^d$, selecting four indices
gives an embedded $B_4(K)$.
Its subsemiring and quotient just constructed establish
\eqref{eq:local-varieties}.
All maps used here preserve the absorbing zero.
head: environment

label: cor:integer-labels
title: Corollary
head: environment
name: Scalar integer labels

title: Proof
body_md:
Use $R=\mathbb Q$ in Lemma~\ref{lem:short-support}.
In the quotient vector space, each difference $[x]-[y]$,
$x\ne y$, and each nonedge sum $[a]+[b]+[c]$ is nonzero.
There are finitely many of these vectors.  Choose a basis and
consider the rational functional
\[
 \ell_t(z_1,\ldots,z_d)=z_1+t z_2+\cdots+t^{d-1}z_d.
\]
For each forbidden vector this is a nonzero polynomial in
$t$, so only finitely many integer values of $t$ are
excluded altogether.  Choose another integer and clear all
denominators.  The resulting integer labels $\lambda_x$
are pairwise distinct and satisfy
$
\lambda_a+\lambda_b+\lambda_c=0\iff abc\in F.
$
The exact Rees construction in the preceding proof now works
in $B_4(\mathbb{Z})$ itself.  The choice uses only the elementary
fact that a nonzero polynomial has finitely many roots.
head: environment

label: lem:capture-criterion
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:capture-criterion}
If $F\subseteq H$ is nonempty, $M\subseteq F$, and
$Z\subseteq E_F$, the same-symbol map embeds
$\langle X\rangle$ into $S_F$.
Moreover some such $F$ has at most $|X|$ stars.
head: environment
name: Capture criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
No operation creates a new letter: a product has type
$p,q,h,0$, and a flat sum retains a summand or gives zero.
Every new $p$- or $q$-element therefore comes from a
product $bc$ or $ab$ of initial letters, hence from a
mandatory star.  The assumptions on $F$ supply every
initial symbol and every newly created $p,q$ index.

The resulting same-symbol map is injective and preserves
zero, which already belongs to every nonempty generated
subsemiring because squares vanish.  Each nonzero edge
product is preserved by $M\subseteq F$.  Products
$ap_a=h$ and $q_cc=h$ depend only on matching symbols
and are also preserved.  A zero product cannot become a
new edge product, since $F\subseteq H$; none of the
symbol-based products changes either.  This proves
multiplicativity, and injectivity with preservation of
zero proves preservation of flat addition.

For the quantitative assertion put $L_M=L\cap E_M$.
Every mandatory star has at least two incidences with
$L_M$, whereas each letter has degree at most two.  Hence
\[
 2|M|\leq\sum_{x\in L_M}\deg_M(x)\leq2|L_M|.
\]
For every $z\in Z\setminus E_M$, choose one incident
retained star.  Together with $M$, these form a set $F$
with
\[
 |F|\leq|M|+|Z\setminus E_M|
 \leq|L_M|+|Z|-|L_M|\leq|X|.
\]
If no star was selected, choose one; $|X|\geq1$ makes the
same bound valid.  All required inclusions hold.
head: environment

label: lem:small-generators
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:small-generators}
For $m\geq2$, every subsemiring of $S_{H_m}$ generated
by at most $4m-1$ elements embeds into some $S_F$ with
\[
 F=V(\Gamma_m)\setminus\{v_0,w\},\qquad v_0=U_0,\quad w\ne v_0.
\]
In particular the local representation theorem applies.
head: environment
name: A second star can be omitted

title: Proof
body_md:
Use the preceding notation for a generating set $X$, with
$|X|\leq4m-1$.  A candidate $w\in H_m$ is permitted if
it is not mandatory and the graph edge $v_0w$, if it
exists, does not belong to $Z$.
For such $w$, every edge in $Z$ has an endpoint in
$F=V(\Gamma_m)\setminus\{v_0,w\}$: an edge lacking one
would have to be $v_0w$.  Also $M\subseteq F$, so
Lemma~\ref{lem:capture-criterion} gives the embedding.

Suppose, to obtain a contradiction, that no candidate is
permitted.  Every retained vertex is then either mandatory
or adjacent to $v_0$ by an edge in $Z$.
Each rung other than $b_0$ has a retained endpoint in the
same bipartition class as $v_0$.  That endpoint is not
adjacent to $v_0$, hence is mandatory.  Its rung is
therefore an actual $B$-letter generator.  At the other
endpoint $\bar U_0$ of $b_0$, either being mandatory or
being forbidden by the edge $b_0\in Z$ also makes $b_0$
a $B$-letter generator: no $p$- or $q$-symbol has a
$B$-index.  Thus $Z$ contains all $2m$ rungs.

Every vertex of the upper cycle except $v_0$ is incident
with a selected $A$- or $C$-index.  For a mandatory
vertex this follows from its definition; otherwise its
forbidden status comes from a selected horizontal edge at
$v_0$.  Every vertex of the lower cycle except
$\bar U_0$ is mandatory and has the same property.
Covering $2m-1$ vertices of a cycle by its edges requires
at least $\lceil(2m-1)/2\rceil=m$ edges.  The two
horizontal cycles are disjoint, so $Z$ contains at least
$2m$ additional indices.  Consequently
\[
 |X|\geq|Z|\geq2m+2m=4m,
\]
contrary to the assumed bound.  A permitted $w$ exists.
For the named-zero language the empty-generated algebra is
$\{0\}$, which needs no embedding construction.

body_md:

title: Proof
body_md:
Take $m=\max\{2,\lfloor k/4\rfloor+1\}$ and
$W_k=S_{H_m}$.  Then $k\leq4m-1$, and
\eqref{eq:witness-size} gives $|W_k|=10m+2$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:prism-identity} supplies an identity valid
in every generator of $\mathcal{B}$, but false in $W_k$.
Hence $W_k\notin\mathcal{B}$.
Every at-most-$k$-generated subsemiring embeds, by
Lemma~\ref{lem:small-generators}, into a two-star-deleted

$\mathsf{V}(B_2(C_r))$ for every $r\geq2$, and in
$\mathsf{V}(B_2(\mathbb{Z}))$.

cyclic subgroup is either $C_r$ for some $r\geq2$, or
$\mathbb{Z}$.  Choosing two indices of $I$ embeds the
corresponding $B_2(\langle g\rangle)$ into $B_I(G)$.
Thus every at-most-$k$-generated subsemiring of $W_k$
belongs to $\mathsf{V}(B_I(G))$.
An evaluation of an identity with at most $k$ variables
lies in the subsemiring generated by its assigned values;
therefore every such identity of $B_I(G)$ holds in
$W_k$.  All embeddings and quotients preserve the
absorbing zero, so the argument includes that constant.

label: thm:full-interval
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:full-interval}
There are inclusions
\[
 \mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathsf{V}(B_2(\mathbb{Z}))\cap
 \bigcap_{p\text{ prime}}\mathsf{V}(B_2(C_p))
 \subseteq\mathcal{B}\subsetneq\mathcal{P}.
\]
Moreover $\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathsf{V}(B_I(G))$ whenever
$|I|\geq2$ and $G\ne\{1\}$.
Every variety $\mathcal W$ with
\[
 \mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathcal W\subseteq\mathcal{P}
\]
has no identity basis with a uniformly bounded number of
variables. This applies to $\mathcal{L}$, $\mathcal{B}$,
$\mathcal{P}$, and the displayed intersection of cyclic
Brandt varieties.
The variety $\mathcal{L}$ is locally finite.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The local representations and the nontrivial cyclic-subgroup
argument prove all inclusions except strictness at the top.
Each small generated subsemiring of $W_k$ embeds into a
generator of $\mathcal{L}$, so belongs to $\mathcal W$.
On the other hand $W_k$ violates its own prism identity,
and hence lies outside $\mathcal{P}$ and outside $\mathcal W$.
This proves the basis assertion for the entire interval.

The generators of $\mathcal{L}$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{eq:nilpotent-laws}
 x^2\approx y^2,\qquad xyzt\approx x^2.
\end{equation}
In the named-zero language they satisfy $x^2\approx0$
and $xyzt\approx0$.
Every semiring term expands, by distributivity, into an
idempotent sum of nonempty multiplicative words.  The laws
\eqref{eq:nilpotent-laws} replace every word of length at
least four by the common square.  On finitely many
generators there are only finitely many words of lengths
at most three and only finitely many subsets to sum.
Thus $\mathcal{L}$ is locally finite.

For strictness, every flat semiring satisfies
\begin{equation}\label{eq:flat-law}
 u+yu+yv\approx v+yu+yv.
\end{equation}
If $u=v$ this is immediate; if $u\ne v$, then
$yu+yv=y(u+v)=0$, which absorbs the remaining sum.
Consider instead the three-element semiring
$D=\{a<b<\infty\}$, with addition maximum, and
\[
 xy=\begin{cases}a,&x,y\in\{a,b\},\\
                  \infty,&\text{otherwise}.
     \end{cases}
\]
Multiplication is associative, and each of its left and
right translations preserves maximum; hence $D$ is an
ai-semiring with absorbing element $\infty$.
It satisfies every prism inequality: if any variable is
$\infty$, it occurs in a retained word, so the right-hand
term is $\infty$ and the inequality holds; otherwise all
triple products are $a$.  But \eqref{eq:flat-law} fails at
$u=b,v=y=a$.  Thus $D\in\mathcal{P}\setminus\mathcal{B}$.
The same example works with $0$ named as $\infty$.

label: thm:linear-variable-complexity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:linear-variable-complexity}
For every variety $\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathcal V\subseteq\mathcal{P}$
and every $N\geq22$,
\[
 4\left\lfloor\frac{N-2}{10}\right\rfloor
 \ \leq\ \nu_{\mathcal V}(N)\ \leq\ N.
\]
Thus the variable complexity grows linearly in $N$,
uniformly throughout this interval, in both signatures.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For the upper bound, take any identity of $\mathcal V$
that fails in an algebra $A$ of size at most $N$.
A witnessing assignment uses at most $N$ distinct elements.
Identify variables assigned the same element, replacing them
by one new variable for each distinct assigned value.
The substituted identity is still valid in $\mathcal V$,
still fails in $A$, and has at most $N$ variables.

For the lower bound, put $m=\lfloor(N-2)/10\rfloor\geq2$.
The prism witness $S_{H_m}$ has $10m+2\leq N$ elements
and lies outside $\mathcal{P}$, hence outside $\mathcal V$.
The local-capture result used in
Theorem~\ref{thm:full-interval} puts every subsemiring of
$S_{H_m}$ generated by at most $4m-1$ elements in
$\mathcal{L}\subseteq\mathcal V$.
It follows that this witness satisfies every identity of
$\mathcal V$ involving at most $4m-1$ variables.
An identity excluding it must therefore use at least $4m$
variables.  This proves the stated lower bound.

label: lem:tree-dual
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:tree-dual}
For every spanning tree $T$ of $Q$, the graph on
$V(\Gamma)$ using exactly the edges outside $T$ is
connected.  Consequently
\begin{equation}\label{eq:colored-bound}
 c(\Gamma)\leq N/2+2.
\end{equation}
If equality holds, the complementary edges themselves
form a spanning tree $T^*$ of $\Gamma$.
The inequality also holds for connected properly
three-colored cubic bipartite multigraphs.
head: environment
name: Tree--dual-tree inequality

title: Proof
body_md:
If the complementary graph were disconnected, take a
nonempty proper vertex set $Y$ equal to one component.
Its nonempty cut $\partial_\Gamma Y$ would consist
entirely of edges of $T$.  At a vertex of $Q$, the
number of incident cut edges is even: around the
corresponding bicolored cycle one enters and leaves
$Y$ equally often.  Thus the cut would be a nonempty
even-degree subgraph of a tree.  This is impossible,
since a nonempty finite forest has a vertex of degree one.
The complementary graph is connected and therefore has
at least $N-1$ edges.  Since $|T|=c(\Gamma)-1$,
\[
 3N/2-(c(\Gamma)-1)\geq N-1,
\]
which gives \eqref{eq:colored-bound}.  Equality makes the
connected complementary graph a tree.  None of this
argument excludes parallel edges in the original graph.
head: environment

label: thm:colored-identity
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:colored-identity}
Suppose
\begin{equation}\label{eq:colored-equality}
 c_{AB}+c_{BC}+c_{CA}=N/2+2.
\end{equation}
Delete any one star $v_0$, put
$\mathbf{u}_\Gamma=\sum_{v\ne v_0}\mathbf{w}_v$, and let
$\mathbf{w}_{v_0}$ be the missing star word.  Then for every
group $G$ and every nonempty Brandt index set $I$,
\[
 B_I(G)\models \mathbf{w}_{v_0}\preceq\mathbf{u}_\Gamma.
\]
head: environment
name: A colored Euler criterion

title: Proof
body_md:
Only an evaluation with $\mathbf{u}_\Gamma\ne0$ needs attention.
Every retained word then has a common value
$(s,\delta,t)$.  Each variable still occurs at its
other graph endpoint, so every variable is nonzero.
The $AB$-cycle through $v_0$, with $v_0$ deleted,
gives a path of retained equations identifying the right
index of the missing $A$-letter with the left index of
its $B$-letter.  The $BC$-cycle gives the other
internal index equality.  The other endpoints of the
missing $A$- and $C$-edges give outside indices
$s,t$.  Thus the identity reduces to equality of the group labels.

Replace every $A$-label $a$ by $\delta^{-1}a$.
All retained triangle products are now $1$.
Choose a spanning tree $T$ of $Q$.  For an oriented
edge $u\to v$, change its label by
\[
 g_{uv}\longmapsto h(u)^{-1}g_{uv}h(v).
\]
Each directed triangle product changes by conjugation
at its starting vertex, so all retained equations with
value $1$ survive.  Choose the $h(u)$ recursively
along $T$ to make every label on $T$ equal to $1$.
This requires only multiplication and inversion in $G$.

By Lemma~\ref{lem:tree-dual}, the complementary edges
form a dual tree $T^*$.  Root it at the missing star.
Process its nonroot leaves toward the root.  At the
current leaf triangle, every edge except its parent
edge is either in $T$, or is a previously processed
child edge, and therefore has label $1$.  The retained
triangle equation forces its parent-edge label to be
$1$.  Induction treats every edge of $T^*$.
Every edge label is now $1$, so the missing triangle
product is $1$ too.  Undoing the label changes gives
its original product $\delta$.  This proves the
identity without a commutativity assumption.
head: environment

label: thm:graph-group-exact
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:graph-group-exact}
For the graph $\Gamma$ above, any choice of the missing
star $v_0$, any group $G$, and any nonempty index set
$I$,
\[
 B_I(G)\models \mathbf{w}_{v_0}\preceq\mathbf{u}_\Gamma
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 G\text{ is abelian}\ \text{or}\ c(\Gamma)=N/2+2.
\]
If $c(\Gamma)<N/2+2$, a counterevaluation exists in
every nonabelian group corner.
head: environment
name: Exact graph--group criterion

label: eq:graph-group-implication
title: Proof
body_md:
For every graph under consideration, the index propagation
and normalization of $A$-labels from the preceding proof
reduce validity to the following implication in $G$:
\begin{equation}\label{eq:graph-group-implication}
 a_vb_vc_v=1\quad(v\ne v_0)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad a_{v_0}b_{v_0}c_{v_0}=1.
\end{equation}
Conversely, failure of this implication yields a Brandt
counterevaluation by putting all labels in a single
diagonal corner.  Every retained word is then $(i,1,i)$;
the missing word is a different nonzero element, and its
addition changes the value to zero.

If $G$ is abelian, give the two bipartition classes
signs $\varepsilon(v)=1,-1$.  In
\[
 \prod_{v\in V(\Gamma)}
       (a_vb_vc_v)^{\varepsilon(v)}
\]
every edge label occurs once positively and once negatively.
The product is $1$, so if all retained factors are $1$,
the missing factor is $1$.  This proves the abelian case.
The case of equality in \eqref{eq:colored-bound} is
Theorem~\ref{thm:colored-identity}.

It remains to disprove \eqref{eq:graph-group-implication}
in a nonabelian group when the inequality is strict.
Choose a spanning tree $T$ of the corner graph $Q$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:tree-dual}, choose a dual spanning tree
$T^*$ of $\Gamma$ using only edges outside $T$.
Identify these dual edges with their variable edges.
There are
\begin{equation}\label{eq:graph-deficit}
 r=\frac{3N}{2}-(c(\Gamma)-1)-(N-1)
   =\frac N2+2-c(\Gamma)>0
\end{equation}
edges outside $T\cup T^*$.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{The polygon obtained from the dual tree.}
Take one abstract triangle for each vertex of $\Gamma$.
Its three corner types are $AB,BC,CA$; its sides are
labelled by its three incident variables.  Pair equal
variable sides, matching their endpoint types.  The
resulting corner classes are precisely the vertices of
$Q$.  Around such a class, the successive triangle
corners follow its bicolored cycle; in particular its
corner link is a single cycle.
Orient the triangles in one bipartition class with
boundary $abc$, and those in the other with boundary
$c^{-1}b^{-1}a^{-1}$.  A paired side is therefore read
in opposite directions by its two triangles.

Initially perform only the side gluings specified by
$T^*$.  They produce a disk: root $T^*$, and attach
each fresh triangle along its unique parent side, making
no further side or vertex identifications at that step.
Its boundary is an edge-paired polygon in which each
edge outside $T^*$ occurs twice, once in each direction.
Pairing the remaining sides recovers the preceding
triangle system.

We need a precise observation about contraction in an
oriented edge-paired polygon.  If a paired side represents
an edge with distinct endpoint vertex classes in the
quotient, deleting its two boundary occurrences merges
exactly these two classes and leaves every other class
unchanged.  Consider the cyclic corner links at the two
endpoints.  Removing the edge
cuts these two distinct cycles into paths.  The new
boundary adjacencies splice the two paths into one cycle,
while all other corner links remain unchanged.  This is
exactly the corner identification induced by deleting
the two side occurrences.

Apply this observation successively to the edges of $T$.
Each such edge still has distinct endpoints when it is
contracted: otherwise its endpoints would already be
joined by contracted edges of the tree, creating a cycle
in $T$.  After all $c(\Gamma)-1$ contractions, the
remaining cyclic boundary word $\mathbf{w}$ has length $2r>0$.
Each of its $r$ letters occurs once positively and once
negatively, and its own side pairing has exactly one
vertex class.  In particular, no extra vertex
identifications are being retained after the $T$-letters
are deleted.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{An interleaving pair of letters.}
The cyclic word $\mathbf{w}$ has no adjacent inverse pair.
For adjacent occurrences $xx^{-1}$, or $x^{-1}x$,
the common polygon corner is identified only with itself:
its two incident sides are the paired occurrences, and
their identification fixes that corner.  It would form
a vertex class separate from the other corners,
contradicting the one-vertex property.

The matching of the two occurrences of each letter around
the boundary must therefore contain two interleaving
pairs.  Indeed, if it were noncrossing, choose a matched
pair with the shortest linear interval between its
endpoints.  If that interval contained an endpoint, its
mate would also lie inside the interval, since otherwise
the pairs would cross.  That would give a shorter matched
interval.  Thus a noncrossing matching has an adjacent
matched pair, which here would be an adjacent inverse pair.

Choose interleaving letters $x,y$.  Assign all other
letters of $\mathbf{w}$ the group identity.  The remaining
word is, up to cyclic rotation,
\[
 x^\epsilon y^\eta x^{-\epsilon}y^{-\eta},
 \qquad \epsilon,\eta\in\{1,-1\}.
\]
Choose noncommuting elements $g,h\in G$ and assign
$x=g,\ y=h$.  Their indicated powers do not commute
either, so this value is nonidentity.  Cyclic rotation
only conjugates a product and cannot change that fact.

\medskip
\noindent\emph{Solving all retained relations.}
Set every $T$-edge label to $1$, and give the edges
outside $T\cup T^*$ the labels just chosen.
Root $T^*$ at the missing triangle.  Process the other
triangles from the leaves towards the root.  At each
step the parent edge is the only undetermined side of
the current triangle; its retained boundary equation
therefore determines that label uniquely.

After these substitutions, the missing boundary product
is the boundary product of the glued disk, up to a
cyclic change of starting point and possible inversion.
This follows one gluing at a time: with compatible
starting points, let the parent boundary read $\mathbf{u}t$
and the child boundary read $t^{-1}\mathbf{v}$.
The child equation gives $t=\mathbf{v}$, so substitution changes
the parent boundary to $\mathbf{u}\mathbf{v}$, exactly the boundary
after gluing.  Repeating this substitution eliminates
all nonroot triangles.
Deleting the $T$-letters now leaves the word $\mathbf{w}$,
because all their labels were $1$.
Thus every retained relation holds, while the missing
boundary has the nonidentity value just constructed,
up to conjugacy or inversion.  This disproves
\eqref{eq:graph-group-implication} in $G$ and completes
the equivalence.

label: cor:abelian-graph
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:abelian-graph}
Suppose $\Gamma$ satisfies the cut condition
\eqref{eq:cut-condition}, without assuming
\eqref{eq:colored-equality}, and let $H$ be obtained by
deleting one star.  Then $|S_H|=5N/2+2$.

head: environment
name: The cut condition over abelian groups

title: Proof
body_md:
The size follows from \eqref{eq:SH-carrier}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:capture-criterion} puts a nonempty
$k$-generated subsemiring into some $S_F$ with
$1\leq|F|\leq k\leq N-2$.
At least two stars are therefore omitted, so the local

label: lem:distinct-cycles
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose a $B$-edge $uv$ joined two vertices of one
$AC$-cycle.  Delete $u,v$, reconnect their two
$A$-neighbors by an $A$-edge, and reconnect their
two $C$-neighbors by a $C$-edge.  Proper coloring
and simplicity ensure that this creates no loops; parallel
edges may occur.  The result is properly colored, cubic,
and bipartite.
It is connected: if $\Gamma-\{u,v\}$ had at least two
components, each would have at least three boundary
edges in $\Gamma$, although only four edges leave
$\{u,v\}$.  This is impossible.

The $AB$- and $BC$-cycles containing $uv$ are
shortened but their numbers do not change.
The vertices $u,v$ have opposite bipartition signs,
so both paths between them on their $AC$-cycle have
odd length.  One has an $A$-edge at each end and the
other a $C$-edge at each end.  The reconnections close
these paths separately, splitting one $AC$-cycle into
two.  Thus the new graph has $N'=N-2$ vertices and
$c'=c(\Gamma)+1$.  It satisfies
\[
 c'-N'/2=(c(\Gamma)+1)-(N-2)/2=4,
\]
contrary to the multigraph version of
Lemma~\ref{lem:tree-dual}.  The supposed edge cannot exist.

label: thm:graph-witness
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:graph-witness}
Suppose $\Gamma$ satisfies the cut condition
\eqref{eq:cut-condition} and the colored equality
\eqref{eq:colored-equality}.  Delete one star to obtain
$H$.  Then
\[
 |S_H|=5N/2+2,\qquad S_H\notin\mathcal{B}.
\]
Every subsemiring of $S_H$ generated by at most $N-1$
elements belongs to $\mathsf{V}(B_2(C_r))$ for every

head: environment
name: Uniform graph witnesses

title: Proof
body_md:
Each color matching has $N/2$ edges, all still appearing
after one star is deleted.  Formula
\eqref{eq:SH-carrier} gives the size.
The natural assignment makes $\mathbf{u}_\Gamma=h$ and the
missing word zero in $S_H$, whereas
Theorem~\ref{thm:colored-identity} gives the identity in
all Brandt semirings.  Hence $S_H\notin\mathcal{B}$.

For the local claim, use the notation $X,Z,L,M$ of
Section~\ref{sec:capture}, with $1\leq|X|\leq N-1$.
The empty-generated algebra in the named-zero language
is $\{0\}$ and already belongs to the required varieties.
As in Lemma~\ref{lem:small-generators}, it suffices to
find a retained vertex $w\notin M$ such that its
possible edge to $v_0$ is not in $Z$.
Suppose no such vertex exists.
Every $B$-edge other than the one at $v_0$ has a
retained endpoint in the same bipartition class as
$v_0$, hence not adjacent to $v_0$.  This endpoint
must be mandatory, forcing the $B$-edge to be an
actual letter generator.  The other endpoint $w_B$
of the $B$-edge at $v_0$ forces that edge too,
either through being mandatory or through its index
being in $Z$.  Thus all $N/2$ $B$-indices lie
in $Z$.

Every vertex outside $\{v_0,w_B\}$ is covered by
an $A$- or $C$-index in $Z$, either because it
is mandatory or because of its selected edge to $v_0$.
By Lemma~\ref{lem:distinct-cycles}, the two exceptions
lie on different even $AC$-cycles.  On either of
these cycles, covering all but one vertex requires at
least half the cycle length in selected edges.  On
every other cycle all vertices are covered, again
requiring at least half the length.  Hence at least
$N/2$ $A/C$-indices lie in $Z$ as well.
This gives $|X|\geq|Z|\geq N$, a contradiction.

A permitted second deletion therefore exists.  The
capture criterion embeds $\langle X\rangle$ into
$S_F$ with exactly two stars omitted.  The local
representation theorem, already proved for every graph
satisfying the cut condition, completes the proof.

label: lem:commutative-hypergraph
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:commutative-hypergraph}
The algebra $C_H$ is a commutative flat ai-semiring.
Every square and every product of four elements is zero.
A product of three elements is nonzero precisely when
its factors are the three vertices of an edge; its value
is then $h$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Linearity makes the multiplication unambiguous.
A nonzero product $(xy)z$ must have $xy=p_z$;
therefore its three factors are vertices forming an
edge, and its value is $h$.
Conversely an edge gives this value in either bracketing.
Every other triple product is zero in both bracketings.
This proves associativity and the asserted triple rule.
The disjoint types in the construction give the square
and four-factor assertions.

For zero-cancellation, fix a vertex $x$.
Equal nonzero products $xy=xy'=p_z$ would give two
edges containing $x,z$, so linearity gives $y=y'$.
The output $h$ occurs only with the factor $p_x$.
A factor $p_x$ has just one nonzero partner, namely $x$.
These observations prove zero-cancellation; commutativity
gives it on both sides.
As in Lemma~\ref{lem:SH}, zero-cancellation is exactly
what is needed for flat addition to distribute.
head: environment

label: lem:commutative-local-representation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:commutative-local-representation}
Let $\Gamma$ satisfy \eqref{eq:cut-condition}, and let
$F$ be a nonempty set of its vertex-stars omitting
at least two graph vertices.  Then
\[
 C_F\in\mathsf{V}(\flat(\mathbb{Z})).
\]
All constructions preserve the absorbing zero.
head: environment

label: eq:commutative-triple-test
title: Proof
body_md:
Use the integral relation module from
\eqref{eq:relation-module} and put
\[
 K=\mathbb{Z}^{E_F}/W_F.
\]
Lemma~\ref{lem:primitive} makes $K$ a finitely generated
free abelian group.  Write $[x]$ for the class of $e_x$.
The short-support lemma shows that distinct vertices have
distinct classes, and, for any three vertices with
repetition allowed,
\begin{equation}\label{eq:commutative-triple-test}
 [x]+[y]+[z]=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \{x,y,z\}\text{ is an edge of }F.
\end{equation}
Indeed, a repeated vertex gives a nonzero integral vector
with support at most two, which cannot belong to $W_F$.
For three distinct vertices, a support-three relation must
be a scalar multiple of a vertex-star.  Its three
coefficients are $1$, so that scalar is $1$.

In the flat extension of the additive group $\mathbb{Z}\times K$,
generate a subsemiring $R$ by zero and
\[
 A_x=(1,[x])\qquad(x\in E_F).
\]
Every nonzero element of $R$ is a nonempty product of
these generators, and its first coordinate is its length.
Let $H_0=(3,0_K)$.
For an incident edge $\{x,y,z\}$,
\[
 A_xA_yA_z=H_0,\qquad
 A_yA_z=(2,-[x])=:P_x.
\]
Thus $H_0$, every $A_x$, and every $P_x$ belong to
$R$ and divide $H_0$.

Adjoin a formal identity for the divisibility criterion, and
let $J$ consist of zero and all elements of $R$
which do not divide $H_0$.
If a product involving an element divides $H_0$,
then that element also divides $H_0$.
Hence $J$ is a multiplicative ideal.
Flat addition also makes $J+R\subseteq J$, so its
Rees quotient is a semiring.

The first coordinate identifies all surviving elements.
At degree one they are the $A_x$.
A degree-two element $A_yA_z$ survives precisely when
some $A_x$ completes it to $H_0$; by
\eqref{eq:commutative-triple-test}, it is then $P_x$.
At degree three only $H_0$ survives, and every element
of degree at least four lies in $J$.
Distinctness within the first two types follows from
$[x]\ne[y]$; their degrees separate the three types.
Finally
\[
 A_xP_y=H_0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad [x]=[y]
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad x=y.
\]
These are exactly the multiplication rules
\eqref{eq:commutative-hypergraph-products}.
The same-symbol correspondence therefore gives
$R/J\cong C_F$.

Since $\mathbb{Z}\times K$ is free abelian of finite rank,
the zero-smash construction gives
$\flat(\mathbb{Z}\times K)\in\mathsf{V}(\flat(\mathbb{Z}))$.
The subsemiring and quotient above prove the assertion.

label: cor:commutative-scalar-representation
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Work in the free abelian group $K$ from the preceding proof.
The forbidden vectors $[x]-[y]$, for $x\ne y$,
and $[x]+[y]+[z]$, for every nonedge triple with
repetitions allowed, are nonzero by the short-support lemma.
There are only finitely many such vectors.
Choose a basis $b_1,\ldots,b_r$ of $K$, and define
$\ell_t(b_i)=t^{i-1}$ for an integer $t$.
For a nonzero vector $v=\sum_i c_i b_i$, the value
$\ell_t(v)=\sum_i c_it^{i-1}$ is a nonzero polynomial
in $t$, so it vanishes at only finitely many integers.
Choose $t$ avoiding the roots for all forbidden vectors,
and put $\lambda_x=\ell_t([x])$.
These integers are pairwise distinct and satisfy
\[
 \lambda_x+\lambda_y+\lambda_z=0
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \{x,y,z\}\text{ is an edge of }F.
\]
Put $L=\max_x|\lambda_x|$, and choose an integer $N>6L$.
In additive notation for $N_+$, generate its flat
subsemiring by the adjoined zero and $N+\lambda_x$, and
retain exactly the divisors of $3N$.
Every generator is positive, and any four generators
have sum at least $4(N-L)>3N$.
The same divisibility argument as above leaves precisely
the values
\[
 N+\lambda_x,\qquad 2N-\lambda_x,\qquad 3N.
\]
The choice of $N$ separates these types.
A pair survives precisely when a third generator makes
an edge, and a generator times a complementary pair
survives precisely for matching indices.
The resulting Rees quotient is $C_F$.

label: lem:commutative-capture
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:commutative-capture}
For every nonempty $X\subseteq C_{H_m}$, there is a
nonempty set $F\subseteq H_m$ of at most $|X|$ stars
such that the same-symbol map embeds
$\langle X\rangle$ into $C_F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $L=X\cap V(H_m)$ be the actual vertex generators.
Let $Z$ consist of their indices and of the indices
$x$ for which $p_x\in X$; $h,0$ contribute no index.
Thus $L\subseteq Z$ and $|Z|\leq|X|$.
Call a retained star mandatory if it contains at least
two members of $L$, and let $M$ be their set.
Writing $L_M=L\cap E_M$, the degree bound two gives
\[
 2|M|\leq\sum_{x\in L_M}\deg_M(x)\leq2|L_M|.
\]
For each $z\in Z\setminus E_M$, choose an incident
retained star, which exists because $H_m$ has no
isolated vertices.  Adjoin these stars to $M$ to
obtain $F$.  Then
\[
 |F|\leq |M|+|Z\setminus E_M|
 \leq |L_M|+|Z|-|Z\cap E_M|\leq |Z|\leq|X|.
\]
If this set is empty, choose one retained star instead.

No operation creates a new vertex.
Every newly generated $p_x$ comes from a product of
two actual vertex generators and hence from a mandatory
star.  Thus $F$ supplies every symbol in $\langle X\rangle$.
It preserves all nonzero vertex-pair products, and the
products $xp_x=h$ depend only on matching symbols.
Since $F\subseteq H_m$, no zero product becomes nonzero.
The same-symbol map therefore preserves multiplication.
It is injective and preserves zero, hence preserves flat
addition as well.
head: environment

label: thm:commutative-uniform
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:commutative-uniform}
For $k\geq1$, put
\[
 m=\max\{2,\lceil(k+2)/4\rceil\},\qquad
 U_k=C_{H_{m}}.
\]
Then $U_k$ is a commutative flat semiring of exactly
$12m+2$ elements, lies outside $\mathcal{P}$, and every
subsemiring generated by at most $k$ elements belongs
to $\mathsf{V}(\flat(\mathbb{Z}))$.
In fact each such subsemiring is a semiring divisor of
$\flat(N_+)$, and hence of $\flat(\mathbb{Z})$.
These statements hold in both signatures.
head: environment
name: Uniform commutative witnesses

title: Proof
body_md:
The size and the failed prism identity were established
in \eqref{eq:commutative-prism-size} and
\eqref{eq:commutative-prism-failure}.
By the capture lemma, a nonempty at-most-$k$-generated
subsemiring embeds in some $C_F$ with $|F|\leq k$.
Since $4m\geq k+2$, at least two prism vertices
lie outside $F$.
Apply Lemma~\ref{lem:commutative-local-representation}.
The stronger divisor assertion follows from
Corollary~\ref{cor:commutative-scalar-representation},
by taking the inverse image of the embedded subsemiring
under its quotient map.
In the named-zero signature the empty-generated algebra
is $\{0\}$, which also has the required property.
head: environment

label: thm:flat-group-all
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:flat-group-all}
Let $G$ be any group.  If $G$ has no finite exponent,
the identities of $\flat(G)$ have no basis with a
uniform finite bound on the number of variables.
For arbitrary $G$,
\[
 \flat(G)\text{ is finitely based}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \begin{gathered}
 G\text{ has finite exponent, and its group}\\
 \text{quasi-equational theory is finitely axiomatizable}.
 \end{gathered}
\]
The equivalence concerns both semiring signatures in
this paper.
head: environment
name: The exact flat-group reduction

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose $G$ has no finite exponent.
For each $d\geq1$, choose $g_d\in G$ with $g_d^d\ne1$.
The tuple $g=(g_d)_{d\geq1}\in G^{\mathbb N}$ has
infinite order: its $d$-th coordinate rules out $g^d=1$.
The cyclic subgroup generated by $g$, together with zero,
and the zero-smash lemma give
\[
 \flat(\mathbb{Z})\in
 \mathsf{V}(\flat(G^{\mathbb N}))\subseteq\mathsf{V}(\flat(G)).
\]
Consequently $U_k$ satisfies every at-most-$k$-variable
identity of $\flat(G)$.
But its prism identity holds in $\flat(G)$ and
fails in $U_k$.  No basis with variable bound $k$
can therefore exist.
For finite exponent, the asserted equivalence is the
established correspondence \cite[Lemma 2.2]{RJZL}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:constant} transfers finite basability to
the named absorbing-zero signature; the witnesses
already preserve that constant.
head: environment

label: cor:commutative-variable-interval
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:commutative-variable-interval}
Every variety
\[
 \mathsf{V}(\flat(N_+))\subseteq\mathcal W\subseteq\mathcal{P}
\]
has no bounded-variable identity basis.  For $N\geq26$,
\[
 4\left\lfloor\frac{N-2}{12}\right\rfloor-1
 \ \leq\ \nu_{\mathcal W}(N)\ \leq\ N.
\]
Thus the variable complexity grows linearly in $N$, and
the uniform term-length bound grows at least linearly.
This applies to the flat extension of every group of
unbounded exponent, in both signatures.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The uniform commutative witness in
Theorem~\ref{thm:commutative-uniform} lies outside
$\mathcal{P}$, whereas each of its at-most-$k$-generated
subsemirings belongs to $\mathsf{V}(\flat(N_+))$.
This excludes any basis with variable bound $k$.
For the quantitative statement put
$m=\lfloor(N-2)/12\rfloor\geq2$.
The witness $C_{H_m}$ has $12m+2\leq N$ elements
and satisfies every identity of $\mathcal W$ in at
most $4m-2$ variables.  An excluding identity therefore
needs at least $4m-1$ variables.
The upper bound follows from the variable-identification
argument in the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:linear-variable-complexity};
the length comparison follows from the definitions.
If $G$ has unbounded exponent, the proof of
Theorem~\ref{thm:flat-group-all} gives
$\flat(\mathbb{Z})\in\mathsf{V}(\flat(G))$, so the lower
inclusion follows from $\flat(N_+)\leq\flat(\mathbb{Z})$.
The upper inclusion follows from the prism identity.
head: environment

label: prop:regular-structure
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:regular-structure}
Every nonzero regular flat semiring is an orthogonal sum
of Brandt semirings.  Equivalently, its multiplicative
semigroup is a primitive inverse semigroup.
head: environment
name: The structure of regular flat semirings

title: Proof
body_md:
Flat distributivity implies zero-cancellation.  Indeed,
if $ab=ac\ne0$ and $b\ne c$, then
$a(b+c)=0$ but $ab+ac=ab\ne0$; the right-sided
argument is the same.
For nonzero idempotents $e,f$ with $ef\ne0$,
\[
 e(ef)=ef=e\cdot f,\qquad (ef)f=ef=e\cdot f.
\]
Cancellation gives $ef=f$ and $ef=e$, respectively.
Thus distinct nonzero idempotents are orthogonal.

Regularity supplies an inverse: replace an inner inverse
$x$ of $a$ by $xax$.  If $b,c$ are both
inverses of nonzero $a$, the nonzero idempotents
$ab,ac$ satisfy $(ab)(ac)=ac$, so $ab=ac$.
Similarly $(ba)(ca)=ba$ gives $ba=ca$.  Hence
\[
 b=bab=(ca)b=c(ab)=c(ac)=cac=c.
\]
Zero has only zero as an inverse.  The semigroup is inverse,
and orthogonality makes every nonzero idempotent primitive.

We give the Brandt coordinates explicitly.
For nonzero $s,t$,
\[
 st=s\,d(s)r(t)\,t,
\]
so it is zero when $d(s)\ne r(t)$.  If these idempotents
agree, then
\[
 (st)(t^{-1}s^{-1})=s\,r(t)\,s^{-1}=ss^{-1}\ne0,
\]
so $st\ne0$.  The nonzero elements therefore form a
groupoid, with exact composability condition
$d(s)=r(t)$.

Partition the nonzero idempotents by $e\sim f$ if some
$s$ has $r(s)=e,d(s)=f$.  This is an equivalence
relation by idempotents, inverses, and composition.
In one component fix $e_0$.  For each $e_i$, choose
$u_i$ with $d(u_i)=e_0,r(u_i)=e_i$, taking
$u_0=e_0$, and let
\[
 G=\{g:d(g)=r(g)=e_0\}.
\]
This is a group.  The map
\[
 (i,g,j)\longmapsto u_i g u_j^{-1}
\]
is a bijection onto the component's nonzero elements: for
$r(s)=e_i,d(s)=e_j$ the inverse label is
$g=u_i^{-1}s u_j$, and $s=u_i g u_j^{-1}$.
It preserves Brandt multiplication, using
$u_j^{-1}u_j=e_0$ and orthogonality when middle indices
differ.  Distinct components multiply to zero.  The
zero-preserving bijection also preserves flat addition.
This proves the claimed decomposition.
head: environment

label: thm:regular-infinite
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:regular-infinite}
Let $S$ be a regular flat semiring whose multiplicative
semigroup is not Clifford.  No cardinality restriction is
imposed.  Then, in either stated language,
\[
 S\text{ is finitely based}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S\text{ is combinatorial}.
\]
In every negative case its identities have no basis with
a uniform variable bound.
head: environment
name: All non-Clifford regular flat semirings

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-structure}, write
$S=\bigoplus^{0} B_{I_\lambda}(G_\lambda)$.
Some index set has size at least two, so
Theorem~\ref{thm:orthogonal} identifies its variety with
$\mathsf{V}(B_2(G))$, where
$G=\prod_\lambda G_\lambda$.
This product group is trivial exactly when every
$G_\lambda$ is trivial.  Now apply
Corollary~\ref{cor:brandt-classification} and
Theorem~\ref{thm:all-groups}.
head: environment

label: thm:finite-regular
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Complete finite regular flat classification

title: Proof
body_md:
Treat the zero-only algebra separately; it satisfies
$x\approx y$ and is finitely based.
Use the decomposition of Proposition~\ref{prop:regular-structure}.
If a block has at least two indices,
Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-infinite} proves the criterion.
If all blocks have one index, the variety is that of
$\flat(G)$, where $G$ is the
finite product of the block groups.  Its Sylow subgroups
are products of the corresponding Sylow subgroups of the
factors, so all are abelian exactly when the condition
holds in every factor.  Apply \eqref{eq:group-criterion}.
For a nonzero combinatorial rank-one sum, both operations
are the same semilattice operation.  It generates the
variety of the two-element semilattice with the operation
duplicated, and is finitely based as well.
head: environment

label: cor:clifford-reduction
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:clifford-reduction}
For an arbitrary Clifford regular flat semiring
$S=\bigoplus^{0} \flat(G_\lambda)$, its finite-basis
problem is exactly that of
$\flat(\prod_\lambda G_\lambda)$.
Writing $G=\prod_\lambda G_\lambda$, this
semiring is finitely based exactly when $G$
has finite exponent and its group quasi-equational theory
is finitely axiomatizable.
If $G$ has no finite exponent, there is no
bounded-variable identity basis.
head: environment
name: The arbitrary-cardinality Clifford reduction

title: Proof
body_md:
The first assertion is Theorem~\ref{thm:orthogonal}.
For finite exponent use \cite[Lemma 2.2]{RJZL}.
The unbounded-exponent assertion follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:flat-group-all}.
Lemma~\ref{lem:constant} treats the absorbing constant.
head: environment

label: thm:clifford-natural
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:clifford-natural}
Let $S$ be a Clifford inverse semigroup with a zero,
at least one nonzero element, and a natural meet operation.
Equip $S$ with this meet as addition.
For each nonzero idempotent $e$, let $G_e$ be its
maximal subgroup, and put
\[
 G=\prod_{e\in E(S)\setminus\{0\}}G_e.
\]
Then $S$ is a subdirect product of the flat semirings
$\flat(G_e)$, and
\[
 \mathsf{V}(S)=\mathsf{V}(\flat(G)).
\]
These assertions hold in both stated signatures, with
no finiteness assumption.
head: environment
name: A subdirect representation for Clifford semirings

title: Proof
body_md:
Idempotents in a Clifford inverse semigroup are central,
and
\[
 d(s)=r(s),\qquad d(st)=d(s)d(t).
\]
For each nonzero idempotent $e$, define
\[
 \pi_e(s)=
 \begin{cases}
 es\in G_e,&e\leq_{\rm nat} d(s),\\
 0,&e\not\leq_{\rm nat} d(s).
 \end{cases}
\]
Here the zero in the codomain is the new element of
$\flat(G_e)$.  Since $e\leq_{\rm nat} d(st)$ holds exactly
when $e\leq_{\rm nat} d(s)$ and $e\leq_{\rm nat} d(t)$, centrality gives
\[
 (es)(et)=est
\]
in the nonzero case, and both sides of the required
multiplicativity equation are zero in every other case.
Thus $\pi_e$ preserves multiplication and zero.

Let $u=s\wedge t$.
If $\pi_e(s)=\pi_e(t)=v\ne0$, then
$v=es=et$ is a common lower bound of $s,t$.
Consequently $v\leq_{\rm nat} u$, so $e=d(v)\leq_{\rm nat} d(u)$ and
$\pi_e(u)=eu=v$.
Conversely, if $\pi_e(u)\ne0$, then $e\leq_{\rm nat} d(u)$;
the inequalities $u\leq_{\rm nat} s,t$ imply
\[
 eu=es=et\ne0.
\]
Therefore, if the two images are different or at least
one is zero, the image of their meet is zero.
This is exactly the flat addition rule in the codomain.
Hence every $\pi_e$ is a semiring homomorphism.
It is onto, because its restriction to $G_e$ is the
identity and it maps the zero of $S$ to zero.

The family separates elements.
A nonzero $s$ is separated from zero by
$\pi_{d(s)}$.
If nonzero $s,t$ have different domains, one of their
domain idempotents is not below the other; the projection
indexed by that idempotent sends one element to a nonzero
value and the other to zero.
If their domains agree, say at $e$, then
$\pi_e(s)=s$ and $\pi_e(t)=t$.
Thus $S$ embeds subdirectly in
$\prod_{e\ne0}\flat(G_e)$.
The surjections give the reverse variety inclusion.
Finally the zero-smash construction and the coordinate
group embeddings give
\[
 \bigvee_{e\ne0}\mathsf{V}(\flat(G_e))
   =\mathsf{V}\left(\flat\left(\prod_{e\ne0}G_e\right)\right),
\]
as in Theorem~\ref{thm:orthogonal}.
This proves the exact formula.
head: environment

label: rem:clifford-nozero
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:clifford-nozero}
If a non-singleton Clifford inverse semigroup $S$ has
natural meets but no zero, the same variety formula holds
in $\{+,\cdot\}$, with the product over all $e\in E(S)$.
Indeed, $S$ has at least two idempotents: otherwise it
would be a group, whose equality natural order cannot
have all binary meets unless it is a singleton.
Distinct idempotents yield comparable distinct idempotents
$p<_{\rm nat}q$, by taking their product if necessary.
Both operations on $\{p,q\}$ are meet.
Assigning an exclusively occurring variable the value
$p$ and all other variables the value $q$ proves that
every valid identity of $S$ has matching variable content.
Adjoining a fresh absorbing zero therefore preserves all
its binary identities.
The resulting $S^0$ is still Clifford and has natural
meets, so Theorem~\ref{thm:clifford-natural} applies.
Since $\mathsf{V}(S)=\mathsf{V}(S^0)$, it gives the asserted formula.
The singleton algebra is treated separately.
head: environment
name: Adjoining an absorbing zero

label: cor:finite-clifford-natural
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:finite-clifford-natural}
\textup{\cite[Theorem 8]{Jackson19}.}
Let $S$ be a finite Clifford inverse semigroup whose
natural order has binary meets, and use these meets as
addition.  Then $S$ is finitely based if and only if
every Sylow subgroup of every maximal subgroup is abelian.
This holds in the binary language and in the language
with its named absorbing zero.
head: environment
name: All finite natural Clifford semirings

title: Proof
body_md:
The singleton case is immediate.
The meet of all elements of the finite set $S$ is a
least element $z$.  Since $z$ is below an idempotent,
it is itself idempotent.  For every $s$, the natural
order relation $z\leq_{\rm nat} s$ gives
\[
 z=s(z^{-1}z)=(zz^{-1})s,
\]
so $sz=zs=z$.  Thus $z$ is a multiplicative zero
and also absorbs meet.
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:clifford-natural} and the finite
flat-group criterion \eqref{eq:group-criterion}.
The product-group Sylow condition is equivalent to the
condition in each factor, as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-regular}.
head: environment

label: cor:clifford-all-basis
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:clifford-all-basis}
Let $S\ne\{0\}$ be a natural Clifford semiring with zero,
of arbitrary cardinality, and put
\[
 G=\prod_{e\in E(S)\setminus\{0\}}G_e.
\]
Then $S$ is finitely based if and only if its maximal
subgroups have a common finite exponent and $G$
has a finitely axiomatizable group quasi-equational theory.
If there is no common finite exponent, $S$ has no
bounded-variable identity basis.
In the binary language the zero assumption can be removed
for non-singleton $S$, using the product over all
idempotents.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:clifford-natural} identifies
$\mathsf{V}(S)$ with $\mathsf{V}(\flat(G))$.
The product group has finite exponent precisely when
its factors have a common finite exponent.
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:flat-group-all} and
Remark~\ref{rem:clifford-nozero}.
head: environment

label: thm:local-clifford-representation
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:local-clifford-representation}
Let $S\ne\{0\}$ be a locally Clifford inverse semigroup
with zero and natural meets.  Then $S$, with natural
meet addition, is a subdirect product of the flat
Brandt semirings $\mathcal{B}_D$ over its nonzero
$\mathcal D$-classes.  In particular
\begin{equation}\label{eq:orthogonalization}
 \mathsf{V}(S)=\bigvee_{D\ne\{0\}}\mathsf{V}(\mathcal{B}_D)
      =\mathsf{V}\left(\bigoplus_{D\ne\{0\}}^{0}\mathcal{B}_D\right).
\end{equation}
All maps preserve zero.
If $S$ is finite, its orthogonal sum on the right has
exactly $|S|$ elements.
head: environment
name: Subdirect Brandt representation

title: Proof
body_md:
First, below any idempotent $e$ there is at most one
idempotent belonging to a specified $\mathcal D$-class.
Otherwise choose distinct $f,g\leq_{\rm nat} e$ in that class
and an arrow $a$ with $d(a)=f,r(a)=g$.
It belongs to $eSe$, but cannot lie in any subgroup,
since its domain and range differ.
This contradicts the Clifford property of $eSe$.

For a nonzero class $D$, define
\[
 \phi_D(s)=
 \begin{cases}
 sf,&\text{if }f\in I_D\text{ and }f\leq_{\rm nat} d(s),\\
 0,&\text{if no such }f\text{ exists}.
 \end{cases}
\]
The preceding uniqueness makes this well-defined.
In the nonzero case $d(sf)=f$, so $sf$ belongs to
$D$, as required.
Every member of $D$ is its own image, and zero maps
to zero; hence $\phi_D$ is onto.

The map $\phi_D$ preserves multiplication.
If $\phi_D(st)\ne0$, choose $h\in I_D$ with
\[
 h\leq_{\rm nat} d(st)=t^{-1}d(s)t.
\]
Then $h\leq_{\rm nat} d(t)$, so $\phi_D(t)=th$.
Its range $g=tht^{-1}$ is an idempotent in $D$
below $d(s)$, giving $\phi_D(s)=sg$.
These two images are composable and their product is
\[
 (sg)(th)=sth=\phi_D(st).
\]
Conversely, suppose $\phi_D(s)=sf$ and
$\phi_D(t)=th$ are nonzero and composable.
The matching condition is $f=tht^{-1}$.
Since $f\leq_{\rm nat} d(s)$, it follows that
$h\leq_{\rm nat} t^{-1}d(s)t=d(st)$; thus
$\phi_D(st)=sth=(sf)(th)$.
We have proved that a product image is nonzero exactly
when the two images have a nonzero product in
$\mathcal{B}_D$, and that their values agree.

Now let $u=s\wedge t$.
If $\phi_D(s)=\phi_D(t)=a\ne0$, then
$a\leq_{\rm nat} s,t$, so $a\leq_{\rm nat} u$.
Its domain lies in $I_D$ below $d(u)$, and the
uniqueness just proved forces $\phi_D(u)=a$.
Conversely, if $\phi_D(u)=a\ne0$, the restrictions
$a\leq_{\rm nat} u\leq_{\rm nat} s,t$ imply
$\phi_D(s)=\phi_D(t)=a$.
This is precisely the flat addition rule, so
$\phi_D$ preserves meet.

Finally suppose all projections of $s,t$ agree.
If $s\ne0$, choose its class $D$.
Then $\phi_D(s)=s=\phi_D(t)$, which implies
$s\leq_{\rm nat} t$.
Interchanging $s,t$ gives the reverse inequality
when both are nonzero.  A nonzero element is also
separated from zero by its own class.
Thus the projections separate elements and give the
claimed subdirect embedding.
Surjectivity gives the reverse variety inclusion;
the orthogonal-sum equality follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:orthogonal}.
The nonzero carriers $D$ partition $S\setminus\{0\}$,
so the orthogonal sum has the same cardinality in the
finite case.

label: cor:local-clifford-all
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:local-clifford-all}
Let $S$ be a non-Clifford locally Clifford inverse
semigroup with zero and natural meet addition, of any
cardinality.  Then $S$ is finitely based if and only
if it is combinatorial.
In every negative case its identities have no basis
with a uniform variable bound.
For a Clifford $S$, the exact flat-group reduction
of Theorem~\ref{thm:clifford-natural} applies instead.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A non-Clifford $S$ has a class $D$ containing at
least two idempotents.
Equations \eqref{eq:orthogonalization} and
\eqref{eq:orthogonal-normal-form} identify its variety
with that of $B_2(\prod_DG_D)$.
This product group is trivial exactly in the
combinatorial case.
Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:brandt-classification}.
head: environment

label: thm:regular-flat-identity
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first prove (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii) in six steps.  The
inverse notation in the proof refers to semigroup inverses
in the multiplicative reduct.

\emph{Step 1: the multiplication is inverse.}
If idempotents $e,f$ belong to the same Green $\mathcal R$-class
or to the same $\mathcal L$-class, then
$efe=e$ and $fef=f$.
Use $(u,v,y,z)=(e,f,e,e)$ in
\eqref{eq:regular-flat-identity} to obtain $e=e+f$, and use
$(e,f,f,f)$ to obtain $e+f=f$.  Hence $e=f$.
Thus each $\mathcal R$-class and each $\mathcal L$-class
contains at most one idempotent.
Regularity supplies an inverse of every element: if $aba=a$,
replace $b$ by $bab$.
If $b,c$ are inverses of $a$, the idempotents $ab,ac$
belong to the $\mathcal R$-class of $a$, and $ba,ca$
belong to its $\mathcal L$-class.  Consequently
$ab=ac$ and $ba=ca$, and
\[
 b=bab=(ca)b=c(ab)=c(ac)=cac=c.
\]
The inverse is unique, as required.

\emph{Step 2: addition of idempotents is their product.}
Let $e,f$ be idempotents; they commute by Step 1.
Substitution $(u,v,y,z)=(e,ef,f,f)$ in
\eqref{eq:regular-flat-identity} gives $e+ef=ef$.
Interchanging $e,f$ gives $f+ef=ef$.
Put $t=e+f$.  Distributivity yields
\[
 et=ft=te=tf=ef,\qquad t^2=ef.
\]
From $et=ft$, multiplication on the right by
$t^{-1}$ gives $er(t)=fr(t)$.  Since idempotents
commute, $r(t)e=r(t)f$, and hence
\[
 t=r(t)t=r(t)(e+f)=r(t)e+r(t)f=r(t)e.
\]
Thus $t$ is idempotent, so $t=t^2=ef$.  We have proved
\begin{equation}\label{eq:idempotent-natural-addition}
 e+f=ef\qquad(e,f\in E(S)).
\end{equation}

\emph{Step 3: the inverse semigroup is locally Clifford.}
Take $a\in eSe$, where $e$ is idempotent, and put
$g=d(a)$, $f=r(a)$.  Both $f,g$ lie below $e$.
For $(u,v,y,z)=(g,e,a,a^{-1})$, both sandwiched
products in \eqref{eq:regular-flat-identity} equal $f$.
Using \eqref{eq:idempotent-natural-addition}, the identity
therefore gives $gf=f$.
Applying the same argument to $a^{-1}$ gives $gf=g$.
Thus $d(a)=r(a)$, so $a$ belongs to a subgroup.
Every local monoid $eSe$ is Clifford.

\emph{Step 4: distinct elements of one subgroup are not
comparable under addition.}
Suppose $g,h\in G_f$ and $g+h=h$, where $f$ is
the identity of this subgroup.  Put $q=g^{-1}h$.
Left multiplication by $g^{-1}$, and then by $q^{-1}$,
gives
\[
 f+q=q,\qquad q^{-1}+f=f.
\]
Now substitute $(u,v,y,z)=(f,q,q^{-1},f)$ in
\eqref{eq:regular-flat-identity}.  Its two sides reduce,
respectively, to $f$ and $q$.  Hence $q=f$ and
$g=h$.

\emph{Step 5: a sum is a natural lower bound.}
Let $t=a+b$ and $e=d(t)$, and define
\[
 x=t^{-1}ae,\qquad y=t^{-1}be.
\]
Then $x,y\in eSe$, and $x+y=t^{-1}te=e$.
In particular $x+e=e$.
By Step 3, $x$ lies in a subgroup with identity
$h=d(x)=r(x)$.  Its inverse also belongs to $eSe$.
Left multiplication of $x+e=e$ by $x^{-1}$ yields
$h+x^{-1}=x^{-1}$.
Step 4 now gives $x^{-1}=h$, so $x=h$ is idempotent.
The same argument makes $y$ idempotent.
Step 2 gives $xy=x+y=e$, while $x,y\leq_{\rm nat} e$ in the
natural order.  It follows that $x=y=e$.
Multiplying $t^{-1}ae=e$ on the left by $t$ gives
\[
 t=tt^{-1}ae=r(t)a\,d(t)\leq_{\rm nat} a.
\]
The last inequality is the natural order: multiplication
by idempotents on either side restricts an inverse-semigroup
element.  Similarly $t\leq_{\rm nat} b$.

\emph{Step 6: this lower bound is the greatest one.}
If $c\leq_{\rm nat} a$ in the natural order, then
\[
 r(c)c\,d(c)=r(c)a\,d(c)=c.
\]
Substitution $(u,v,y,z)=(c,a,r(c),d(c))$ in
\eqref{eq:regular-flat-identity} gives $c+a=c$.
If $c\leq_{\rm nat} a,b$, we therefore have
$c+t=c+(a+b)=c$.
By Step 5, applied to the pair $c,t$, its sum $c$
lies naturally below $t$.  Thus $t=a\wedge b$,
completing (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii).

For (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii), apply the subdirect Brandt
representation in Theorem~\ref{thm:local-clifford-representation}.
If a zero is absent in the binary language, the zero-adjunction
argument following Corollary~\ref{cor:local-clifford-all}
preserves all identities and reduces to that theorem.
The one-element case is immediate.

Finally every flat semiring satisfies
\eqref{eq:regular-flat-identity}.  If $u=v$, the two
sides agree.  Otherwise $u+v=0$, so
$yuz+yvz=y(u+v)z=0$, which absorbs the remaining sum.
The identity is preserved under homomorphic images,
subalgebras and products.  This proves (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i).

label: lem:brandt-monoid-divisor
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:brandt-monoid-divisor}
Let $S$ be a finite inverse semigroup with natural
meet addition.  If $S$ is not locally Clifford,
then the naturally semilattice-ordered Brandt monoid $B_2^1$
is a subsemiring of a homomorphic image of a
subsemiring of $S$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The least element of $S$ is an absorbing zero, by
the argument in Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-clifford-natural}.
Choose $e$ such that the finite inverse monoid
$M=eSe$ is not Clifford.
It is closed under natural meet: a restriction of
an element of $eSe$ again has domain and range
below $e$.
Choose in $M$ an element with different domain and
range, and let $D$ be its $\mathcal D$-class.
Thus $D$ has at least two idempotents and is not the
class of units of $M$.

We use two elementary finite-semigroup facts.
First, $\mathcal D=\mathcal J$ in a finite semigroup.
Consequently, for $J=MDM$, the set $I=J\setminus D$
is an ideal of $M$.
Second, naturally comparable elements in one
$\mathcal D$-class of a finite inverse semigroup
are equal.
For the latter assertion it suffices first to consider
idempotents $f\leq_{\rm nat} g$ in one class.
An arrow between them gives mutually inverse bijections
of the principal right ideals $fM$ and $gM$.
But $fM\subseteq gM$, and if $f\ne g$, then
$g\notin fM$, contradicting equality of their finite
cardinalities.
For $a\leq_{\rm nat} b$ in one class, apply this to
$d(a)\leq_{\rm nat} d(b)$; their equality gives $a=b$.

Put $R=J\cup\{e\}$.  Here $e\notin J$, since the
chosen class is not the class of units.
The set $R$ is closed under multiplication.
It is closed under meet as well: an element below a
member of $J$ belongs to that ideal.
The same observation shows that $i\wedge r\in I$
for $i\in I,r\in R$.
Thus collapsing $I$ is a semiring Rees quotient.

The multiplicative quotient $J/I=D\cup\{0\}$ is
the Brandt principal factor $B_n(G)$, with $n\geq2$.
One may see its coordinates directly from the arrows
between the idempotents of $D$: a nonmatching product
must lie below $D$, by the comparability fact, and
matching products are groupoid composition.
The image of $e$ adjoins an identity.
Distinct elements of $D$ have their meet in $I$,
again by comparability.
Also $e\wedge a=a$ for idempotent $a\in D$;
for nonidempotent $a\in D$, this meet lies in $I$,
because an element below $e$ is idempotent.
These are exactly the natural meet rules in
$B_n^1(G)$.  Hence
\[
 R/I\cong (B_n^1(G),+_{\rm nat},\cdot).
\]
Choose two indices, the identity group labels, the
zero, and the adjoined identity.
They form the required subsemiring $B_2^1$.
All constructions preserve the absorbing zero.
