label: lem:s7-snfb
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:s7-snfb}
The three-element semiring $S_7$ is strongly nonfinitely
based in the binary ai-semiring language.  Equivalently,
\[
 T\text{ finite},\quad S_7\in\mathsf{V}(T)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad T\text{ is nonfinitely based}.
\]
head: environment

label: lem:s7-transfer
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:s7-transfer}
If a finite ai-semiring $A$ satisfies $S_7\in\mathsf{V}(A)$,
then $A$ is itself SNFB.  Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-snfb} also holds
after naming the existing absorbing zero of $S_7$,
among ai-semirings with a named absorbing zero.
More generally, if $\mathsf{V}(A)=\mathsf{V}(T)$ for a finite $T$,
then $S_7\in\mathsf{V}(A)$ implies that $A$ is nonfinitely
based, whether or not $A$ is finite.
head: environment
name: Transfer and the absorbing constant

title: Proof
body_md:
If $A\in\mathsf{V}(T)$, transitivity gives $S_7\in\mathsf{V}(T)$;
apply Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-snfb} when $T$ is finite.
The assertion about equal varieties is the same argument.

For the signature assertion let finite $(T;0)$ generate
a variety containing $(S_7;0)$, where the notation means
that the existing zero is named.  Its binary reduct already
has $S_7$ in its variety.  Lemma~\ref{lem:constant}
equates finite basability in the two signatures, and
Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-snfb} gives the result.
head: environment

label: lem:s7-sandwich
title: Lemma
head: environment
name: A separating sandwich identity

title: Proof
body_md:
In a Brandt semiring, $x^r$ is either zero or a diagonal
matrix idempotent $e_i=(i,1,i)$.  In the latter case,
if $y$ belongs to the group at $i$, then
$y^{r+1}=y$.  If $y$ does not belong to that group,
both sandwiched products are zero: a different diagonal
corner stays different, and a nonzero off-diagonal element
has square zero.  This proves the identity, including all
zero assignments.  In $S_7$, take $x=1,y=a$; the two
sides are $a$ and $0$.
head: environment

label: thm:s7-finite-detection
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:s7-finite-detection}
For a finite natural inverse semiring $S$,
\[
 S_7\in\mathsf{V}(S)
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S\text{ is not locally Clifford}.
\]
Every finite natural inverse semiring that is
not locally Clifford is SNFB and hence nonfinitely based.
head: environment
name: Varieties containing $S_7$

title: Proof
body_md:
If $S$ is not locally Clifford, the divisor in
Lemma~\ref{lem:brandt-monoid-divisor} contains
\[
 \{1,e_{12},0\}\cong S_7:
 \qquad e_{12}^2=0,\quad1+e_{12}=0.
\]
Thus $S_7\in\mathsf{V}(S)$, with the zero preserved.
If $S\ne\{0\}$ is locally Clifford, choose a common
multiple $r\geq2$ of the exponents of its finitely many
maximal subgroups.  Its Brandt factors in
Theorem~\ref{thm:local-clifford-representation} satisfy
\eqref{eq:s7-sandwich}, and therefore so does $S$.
The lemma excludes $S_7$ from its variety.
The zero-only case is immediate.
The SNFB assertion follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-transfer}.
head: environment

label: thm:finite-natural-classification
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:finite-natural-classification}
Let $S$ be a finite inverse semigroup whose natural
order has binary meets, and use them as addition.
In either $\{+,\cdot\}$ or $\{+,\cdot,0\}$,
$S$ is finitely based if and only if at least one
of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}[$(\rm i)$]
\item $S$ is locally Clifford and combinatorial;
\item $S$ is Clifford and all Sylow subgroups of
every maximal subgroup are abelian.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: All finite natural inverse semirings

title: Proof
body_md:
The singleton case is immediate; otherwise $S$
has its natural absorbing zero.
If $S$ is locally Clifford, its orthogonalization
in Theorem~\ref{thm:local-clifford-representation}
is a finite regular flat semiring with exactly the
same identities.  Its group factors and its classes
with two or more idempotents retain precisely those
features of $S$.  Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-regular}
therefore gives alternatives (i) and (ii).
If $S$ is not locally Clifford,
Theorem~\ref{thm:s7-finite-detection} and
Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-snfb} give nonfinite basability directly.
head: environment

label: cor:finite-natural-brandt-variety
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:finite-natural-brandt-variety}
For a finite natural inverse semiring $S$,
\[
 S\in\mathcal{B}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S\text{ is locally Clifford}.
\]
head: environment
name: A membership characterization

title: Proof
body_md:
The subdirect representation proves membership in
the locally Clifford case.
Otherwise the divisor lemma would place $B_2^1$
in $\mathcal{B}$, contrary to the explicit failure of
the prism identities in Section~\ref{sec:boundary}.
head: environment

label: thm:s7-exponent
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
A diagonal corner gives (i)$\Rightarrow$(ii).
Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-sandwich} gives (ii)$\Rightarrow$(iii),
taking a multiple $r\geq2$ of a finite exponent if necessary.
For (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i), choose for every $m\geq1$
an element $g_m\in G$ with $g_m^m\ne1$.
Then $g=(g_m)_{m\geq1}\in G^{\mathbb N}$ has infinite
order, because its $d$-th coordinate rules out $g^d=1$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:smash} gives
\[
 \flat(G^{\mathbb N})\in\mathsf{V}(\flat(G)).
\]
In this semiring take the subsemiring
$T=\{0\}\cup\{g^j:j\geq0\}$ and its ideal
$J=\{0\}\cup\{g^j:j\geq2\}$.
All powers displayed are distinct.  The semiring Rees
quotient $T/J$ has the two nonzero elements $1,g$,
with $g^2=0$, and flat addition.  It is $S_7$.
These constructions all preserve the absorbing zero.
head: environment

label: cor:s7-local-exponent
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:s7-local-exponent}
Let $S\ne\{0\}$ be a locally Clifford inverse
semigroup with zero and natural meet addition, of any
cardinality.  Then $S_7\in\mathsf{V}(S)$ if and only if
its maximal subgroups have no common finite exponent.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Put $G=\prod_DG_D$, taking one maximal subgroup in
each nonzero $\mathcal D$-class.  Theorems
\ref{thm:local-clifford-representation} and
\ref{thm:orthogonal} identify $\mathsf{V}(S)$ with either
$\mathsf{V}(\flat(G))$ or $\mathsf{V}(B_2(G))$.
The group $G$ has exponent dividing $r$ exactly
when every factor does.  Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:s7-exponent}.
head: environment

label: lem:locally-finite-rank
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:locally-finite-rank}
In a finite signature, a locally finite variety is finitely
based if and only if it has an identity basis with a uniform
finite bound on the number of variables.
Consequently every finite nonfinitely based algebra has
no bounded-variable identity basis.
head: environment
name: Variable bounds in locally finite varieties

title: Proof
body_md:
Only the reverse direction needs proof.  Suppose a basis
uses at most $k$ variables.  The relatively free algebra
$F_{\mathcal V}(k)$ is finite.  Choose a representing
$k$-variable term $\mathbf{t}_a$ for each of its elements $a$.
For every basic operation $f$ and every tuple of elements,
take the valid identity
\[
 f(\mathbf{t}_{a_1},\ldots,\mathbf{t}_{a_m})\approx \mathbf{t}_{f(a_1,\ldots,a_m)},
\]
together with $x_i\approx \mathbf{t}_{[x_i]}$; nullary operations,
if present, are included in the same way.
This is a finite family of identities valid in $\mathcal V$.
Induction on a term reduces every $k$-variable term to
the representative of its value in the free algebra.
Thus this finite family entails every valid $k$-variable
identity and hence the proposed bounded-variable basis.
It is a finite basis for $\mathcal V$.
head: environment

label: thm:three-obstructions
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $S$ is not locally Clifford, (i) follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:s7-finite-detection}.
If $S$ is locally Clifford but not Clifford and is
nonfinitely based, it has a nontrivial maximal subgroup.
The orthogonalization and product-group formula put
$B_2(C_p)$ in its variety for a prime divisor $p$
of the order of such a subgroup.
If $S$ is Clifford and nonfinitely based, its finite
flat-group reduction has a nonabelian Sylow subgroup;
the corresponding flat group is a divisor in its variety.
This proves necessity using
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-natural-classification}.

Condition (i) implies nonfinite basability by Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-snfb}.  Condition (iii) does so by
\cite[Theorem 6.1]{JRZ}, which states that every finite
ai-semiring whose variety contains a finite ai-semiring
with a nonabelian nilpotent subgroup is nonfinitely based.
For (ii), if $S$ were finitely based, its two
possible structures in
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-natural-classification} would
both exclude $B_2(C_p)$: a locally Clifford
combinatorial $S$ satisfies $x^2\approx x^3$,
while a finite Clifford $S$ satisfies
$x^{r+1}\approx x$ for a common group exponent $r$.
The first fails in its nontrivial group corner and the
second fails at an off-diagonal element of $B_2(C_p)$.

To show that no alternative can be omitted, use,
respectively, $B_2^1$,
$B_2(C_p)$, and $\flat(P)$.
The first satisfies $x^2\approx x^3$, excluding
both types of nontrivial-group obstruction.
The second excludes $S_7$ by the sandwich identity;
it also satisfies
\[
 x^{p+2}\approx x^2,\qquad
 x^{p+1}y^{p+1}\approx y^{p+1}x^{p+1}.
\]
The latter identity holds because each $(p+1)$-st
power is zero or stays in an abelian diagonal group.
Any group whose flat extension belongs to this variety
must therefore have exponent dividing $p$ and be abelian.
Finally $\flat(P)$ satisfies $x^{r+1}\approx x$,
where $r$ is its exponent; this excludes both $S_7$
and every $B_2(C_q)$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
The three obstructions cannot be combined arbitrarily:
\textup{(i)} and \textup{(iii)} together imply
\textup{(ii)}.  Indeed, \textup{(i)} gives a natural
$B_2^1$ divisor and hence $B_2\in\mathsf{V}(S)$.
Condition \textup{(iii)} gives $\flat(C_p)\in\mathsf{V}(S)$.
The Brandt join formula then puts $B_2(C_p)$ in
$\mathsf{V}(S)$.

label: cor:relative-natural-transfer
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:relative-natural-transfer}
Let $A,B$ be finite natural inverse semirings
with $A\in\mathsf{V}(B)$.  If $A$ is nonfinitely based,
then $B$ is nonfinitely based.
Equivalently, every finite natural inverse member of the
variety generated by a finitely based finite natural
inverse semiring is finitely based.
head: environment
name: Transfer within the finite natural inverse class

title: Proof
body_md:
One of the three obstructions in
Theorem~\ref{thm:three-obstructions} belongs to $\mathsf{V}(A)$,
and therefore to $\mathsf{V}(B)$.  Apply the same theorem to
$B$.
head: environment

label: cor:finite-regular-identity
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:finite-regular-identity}
Let $S$ be a finite ai-semiring with regular multiplication
satisfying \eqref{eq:regular-flat-identity}.
Then $S$ is finitely based if and only if either
\begin{enumerate}[$(\rm i)$]
\item its multiplicative semigroup is combinatorial; or
\item its multiplicative semigroup is Clifford and every
Sylow subgroup of every maximal subgroup is abelian.
\end{enumerate}
This holds in both signatures considered here.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-flat-identity} makes $S$ a
locally Clifford natural inverse semiring.
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-natural-classification}.
head: environment

label: cor:relative-regular-transfer
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:relative-regular-transfer}
Let $B$ be a finitely based finite regular ai-semiring
satisfying \eqref{eq:regular-flat-identity}.
Every finite member $A\in\mathsf{V}(B)$ whose multiplication
is regular is finitely based.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The identity passes from $B$ to $A$, so both are
natural inverse semirings by
Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-flat-identity}.
Apply Corollary~\ref{cor:relative-natural-transfer}.
head: environment

label: prop:flat-local-s7
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:flat-local-s7}
Let $S$ be any finite flat ai-semiring.  If for some
nonzero idempotent $e$, the local monoid $eSe$
has a nonzero nonunit, then $S$ contains $S_7$
as a subsemiring.  Moreover, $S$
is SNFB and hence nonfinitely based.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The local monoid $M=eSe$ is a flat subsemiring with
unit $e$ and zero $0$.
The structural step is \cite[Proposition 2.4]{JRZ}
applied to $M$; we include its short argument.
It has no nonzero idempotent other than $e$: if
$f^2=f\ne0$, then $ef=ff\ne0$, and zero-cancellation
gives $e=f$.
For a nonzero nonunit $b$, finiteness gives an
idempotent power.  This cannot be $e$, since
$b^m=e$ would make $b$ a unit of $M$.
Thus some power is zero.  If $b^j$ is the last
nonzero power, set $a=b^j$.  Then $a^2=0$,
and $\{e,a,0\}\cong S_7$ with flat addition.
The conclusion follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-transfer}.
head: environment

label: thm:seven
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:seven}
Among finite flat semirings with regular multiplication,
the smallest nonfinitely based cardinality is seven.
Up to isomorphism there is exactly one such seven-element
semiring:
\[
 R_7=B_2\oplus^{0} \flat(C_2).
\]
Its variety is $\mathsf{V}(B_2(C_2))$.
head: environment
name: The smallest nonfinitely based regular example

title: Proof
body_md:
The variety assertion follows from
Theorem~\ref{thm:orthogonal}, so $R_7$ is nonfinitely
based.  Its two blocks have four and two nonzero elements,
and share one zero.

In a finite Clifford negative case,
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-regular} forces a nonabelian Sylow
subgroup.  A group of order $p$ or $p^2$ is abelian,
so a nonabelian $p$-group has order at least $p^3\geq8$.
Such a block already contributes at least nine elements
including zero.
In a non-Clifford negative case a rank-at-least-two block
and a nontrivial group are both required.  If in one block,
they give at least $2^2\cdot2=8$ nonzero elements.
If in different blocks, they give at least $4+2=6$.
Equality at total size seven forces exactly the displayed
two blocks and no others.
head: environment

label: thm:cyclic-minimum
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:cyclic-minimum}
Let $r\geq2$ and write
\[
 r=\prod_{i=1}^s q_i,\qquad q_i=p_i^{a_i},
\]
where the primes $p_i$ are distinct and $a_i\geq1$.
Among all finite regular flat semirings generating
$\mathsf{V}(B_2(C_r))$, the minimum size is
\[
 5+\sum_{i=1}^s q_i.
\]
Up to isomorphism the unique minimum generator is
\[
 B_2\oplus^{0}\flat(C_{q_1})\oplus^{0}\cdots
       \oplus^{0}\flat(C_{q_s}).
\]
In particular, for a prime power $r=p^a$ the minimum is
$p^a+5$, uniquely attained by
$B_2\oplus^{0} \flat(C_{p^a})$.
head: environment
name: Unique minimum cyclic-variety generators

title: Proof
body_md:
The displayed semiring has the required variety because
$C_r\cong\prod_i C_{q_i}$ and
Theorem~\ref{thm:orthogonal} applies.
Let a finite regular flat semiring $A$ generate that
same variety, and write its Brandt blocks as
$B_{n_\lambda}(G_\lambda)$.
The target satisfies $x^{r+2}\approx x^2$: on a
diagonal element this is the exponent law, and on an
off-diagonal element both sides are zero.  In a corner
group of $A$, cancellation therefore gives exponent
dividing $r$.

For each $i$, the target fails
$x^{r/p_i+2}\approx x^2$, so $A$ fails it too.
Off-diagonal elements cannot witness this failure; hence
some corner contains an element whose order has full
$p_i$-part $q_i$, and therefore contains an element
of order $q_i$.  Assign requirement $q_i$ to one
such block.  A group supporting a set $Q$ of assigned
requirements has order at least $\prod_{q\in Q}q$,
by Lagrange's theorem.  For two or more distinct prime
powers their product is strictly greater than their sum;
for a singleton it equals that requirement.

There must also be a block with $n_\lambda\geq2$.
Otherwise every element lies in a group of exponent
dividing $r$ or is zero, and $x^{r+1}\approx x$
would hold in $A$, contrary to its failure on an
off-diagonal element of $B_2(C_r)$.
Choose one such block.  It contributes at least four
nonzero elements in addition to the sum of its assigned
requirements, strictly more if any requirement is
assigned there: for a nonempty assignment,
$4\prod Q>4+\sum Q$.
Every other block contributes at least the sum of its
assigned requirements, with strict inequality if it has
none or more than one, or if its rank exceeds one.
Summing gives at least
$4+\sum_iq_i$ nonzero elements.

Equality forces one trivial-group rank-two block with no
assigned requirement, and one rank-one group of order
$q_i$ for each requirement.  Such a group contains an
element of its full order $q_i$, so it is cyclic.  No
additional blocks are possible.  This proves both
minimality and uniqueness.
head: environment

label: cor:cyclic-natural-minimum
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:cyclic-natural-minimum}
For $r=\prod_iq_i\geq2$ as in
Theorem~\ref{thm:cyclic-minimum}, the minimum size of
a finite natural inverse semiring generating
$\mathsf{V}(B_2(C_r))$ is still
\[
 5+\sum_iq_i.
\]
The orthogonalization of every minimum generator is
the unique flat generator in that theorem.
The minimum generator itself need not be unique once
flatness is removed.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Any such generator belongs to $\mathcal{B}$, so is
locally Clifford by
Corollary~\ref{cor:finite-natural-brandt-variety}.
Its orthogonalization has the same size and variety.
Theorem~\ref{thm:cyclic-minimum} gives the lower bound
and the asserted orthogonalization.
The flat example there attains the bound.

For nonuniqueness take $r=2$, let
$C_2=\{1,g\}$, and consider the following
seven-element subset of
$B_2\times \flat(C_2)$:
\[
 A=\{(e_{ij},1):1\leq i,j\leq2\}
       \cup\{(0,1),(0,g),(0,0)\}.
\]
It is closed under multiplication, inversion, and
coordinatewise natural meet.
Products of matrix-unit pairs that do not match
give $(0,1)$; operations with the last three
elements stay in the displayed set.
Both coordinate projections are onto.
Hence
\[
 \mathsf{V}(A)=\mathsf{V}(B_2)\vee\mathsf{V}(\flat(C_2))
      =\mathsf{V}(B_2(C_2)).
\]
Its zero is $(0,0)$, while
$(e_{11},1)+(e_{22},1)=(0,1)\ne(0,0)$.
Thus $A$ is nonflat and cannot be isomorphic to
the flat minimum $R_7$.
head: environment

label: thm:smallest-natural
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:smallest-natural}
The smallest
nonfinitely based finite natural inverse
semiring has six elements and is uniquely $B_2^1$,
up to isomorphism.
Among the $S_7$-free members of this class the
smallest nonfinitely based size is seven.
There are exactly four isomorphism types at that size,
and all four generate $\mathsf{V}(B_2(C_2))$.
Consequently they are also exactly the minimum finite
natural inverse-semiring generators of that variety.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
An $S_7$-free finite member is locally Clifford by
Theorem~\ref{thm:s7-finite-detection}.
Its orthogonalization has the same size and identities;
Theorem~\ref{thm:seven} gives the lower bound seven,
with orthogonalization necessarily $R_7$ at equality.
A non-locally-Clifford member has $B_2^1$ as a
semiring divisor and therefore has at least six elements.
The six-element $B_2^1$ contains $S_7$, so is
nonfinitely based by Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-snfb}.
If a six-element $S$ has this divisor, restrict the
quotient map to the inverse image of that subsemiring.
The resulting surjection from a subsemiring of $S$
onto $B_2^1$ must be a bijection on all of $S$.
This proves the six-element assertion.

We now describe and classify the seven-element cases.
Put $C_2=\{1,g\}$, and work inside
$P=B_2\times \flat(C_2)$, with coordinatewise
natural meet. We identify $R_7$ with its coordinate-axis
copy. The four subsemirings are
\begin{align*}
 R_7&=\{(e_{ij},0):1\leq i,j\leq2\}
             \cup\{(0,1),(0,g),(0,0)\},\\
 R_t&=\{(e_{11},1),(e_{22},1),(e_{12},t),(e_{21},t)\}
             \cup\{(0,1),(0,g),(0,0)\},
             \quad t\in\{1,g\},\\
 R'_7&=\{(e_{ij},0):1\leq i,j\leq2\}
             \cup\{(e_{11},1),(e_{11},g),(0,0)\}.
\end{align*}
The other three semirings are nonflat.

For closure of $R_t$, matching matrix products have
the displayed labels because $1t=t$ and $t^2=1$.
Nonmatching products have first coordinate zero and
land in its last three elements, as do all products
involving those elements.  Inversion interchanges the
off-diagonal entries, with $t^{-1}=t$.
The meet of distinct matrix elements has first
coordinate zero, so it too is retained.
For $R'_7$, the four matrix-axis elements,
together with $(0,0)$, form $B_2$.
The two additional nonzero elements have the same
first coordinate $e_{11}$, and form a group of
order two; their products with the other elements
stay on the matrix axis.  Their meet is $(e_{11},0)$,
and their meets with any other matrix element are
$(e_{11},0)$ or $(0,0)$, as appropriate.
The axis construction proves closure for $R_7$.
Thus all four are inverse subsemigroups closed under
the ambient natural meet, with that meet as their own
natural meet.  Both coordinate projections are onto.
Hence all four generate
\[
 \mathsf{V}(B_2)\vee\mathsf{V}(\flat(C_2))
 =\mathsf{V}(B_2(C_2)),
\]
so are nonfinitely based and $S_7$-free.

Let $S$ be any seven-element
$S_7$-free nonfinitely based member.
Its orthogonalization is $R_7$, so its nonzero
$\mathcal D$-classes are
\[
 M=\{e,f,a,b\},\qquad H=\{h,g\}\cong C_2,
\]
where $e,f$ are the two matrix idempotents, $a,b$
are inverse connecting arrows, and $h$ is the unit
of $H$.  The two projections of
Theorem~\ref{thm:local-clifford-representation} embed
$S$ into $B_2\times \flat(C_2)$.
The idempotents $e,f$ are incomparable and cannot
both lie below $h$, by local Cliffordness.
If $h\leq_{\rm nat} e$, conjugating by a connecting arrow
gives an idempotent in the class $H$ below $f$.
It must be $h$, the unique idempotent of $H$.
Thus $h\leq_{\rm nat} e$ implies $h\leq_{\rm nat} f$, and conversely.
Up to exchanging $e,f$, the only possible orders are
\begin{enumerate}[$(\rm a)$]
\item $e,f,h$ pairwise incomparable;
\item $h<_{\rm nat}e$ and $h<_{\rm nat}f$;
\item $e<_{\rm nat}h$, with $f$ incomparable to $h$.
\end{enumerate}
In (a) the cross-class restrictions all vanish, so the
projection image is $R_7$.
In (b), the $H$-coordinates of $e,f$ are both
$1$.  The coordinate of $a$ is a value
$t\in\{1,g\}$, and that of $b$ is $t^{-1}=t$.
The matrix coordinates of $h,g$ vanish, giving
exactly $R_1$ or $R_g$.
In (c), all $H$-coordinates of $M$ vanish.
Both $h,g$ project to $e_{11}$, since their
restriction lies in the trivial group there.
This gives exactly $R'_7$.
The injective projections determine the full operations,
so there are no further cases or parameters.

The orders (a), (b), (c) have, respectively, three,
one, and two nonzero minimal idempotents, distinguishing
the three families.  In $R_1$ and $R_g$, the two
off-diagonal elements are the only elements outside
all subgroups.  Their sum is the idempotent $h$
in $R_1$, but the nonidempotent $g$ in $R_g$.
Thus these two are also nonisomorphic.
The final minimum-generator assertion follows from
Corollary~\ref{cor:cyclic-natural-minimum} at $r=2$.

label: thm:product-fb
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:product-fb}
Let $S_1,\ldots,S_t$, $t\geq1$, be finite
natural inverse semirings.
Their direct product is finitely based if and only if
either
\begin{enumerate}[$(\rm i)$]
\item every $S_i$ is locally Clifford and combinatorial;
or
\item every $S_i$ is Clifford, and every Sylow subgroup
of every maximal subgroup of every $S_i$ is abelian.
\end{enumerate}
The same criterion holds for their orthogonal sum and
for the finite join $\bigvee_i\mathsf{V}(S_i)$.

In particular, if all factors are finitely based, their
product is finitely based exactly when all factors are
combinatorial or all factors are Clifford.
It is nonfinitely based exactly when some factor is
non-Clifford and some other factor has a nontrivial subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The product has natural meets coordinatewise.
Cliffordness, local Cliffordness, and being combinatorial
hold in the product precisely when they hold in every
factor; local monoids and maximal subgroups are the
corresponding direct products.  The Sylow subgroups of
a finite product group are the products of its Sylow
subgroups, so their being abelian is also coordinatewise.
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-natural-classification}.
The product generates the join of the factor varieties.
Their orthogonal sum embeds on the coordinate axes,
because zero absorbs both operations; each summand also
embeds in that sum.  Hence it generates the same join.
If the factors are already finitely based, they are all
locally Clifford and all their maximal subgroups have
abelian Sylow subgroups.  The criterion reduces to the
last assertion.  The two offending features cannot occur
in one factor, since that factor would not be finitely based.
head: environment

label: cor:inverse-monoid-fb
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:inverse-monoid-fb}
A finite inverse monoid with natural meet addition is
finitely based if and only if it is Clifford and every
Sylow subgroup of every maximal subgroup is abelian.
head: environment
name: Finite natural inverse monoids

title: Proof
body_md:
A monoid is locally Clifford only if it is Clifford,
by taking its global identity as the corner idempotent;
the converse holds as well.
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-natural-classification}.
head: environment

label: thm:arbitrary-local-family
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:arbitrary-local-family}
Let $(S_\lambda)_{\lambda\in\Lambda}$ be a nonempty family
of locally Clifford inverse semigroups with natural meet
addition, with no cardinality restrictions on the family or
its members.  Put
$\mathcal W=\bigvee_\lambda\mathsf{V}(S_\lambda)
             =\mathsf{V}(\prod_\lambda S_\lambda)$.
If every factor is one-element, $\mathcal W$ is trivial.
Otherwise discard one-element factors and, in the binary
language, adjoin a zero to any remaining factor lacking one.
These changes preserve $\mathcal W$.
For these factors put
\[
 G = \prod_{\lambda\in\Lambda}
       \prod_{D\ne\{0\}}G_{\lambda,D},
\]
where one maximal subgroup is chosen in each nonzero
$\mathcal D$-class of $S_\lambda$.
Then
\[
 \mathcal W=\mathsf{V}\left(\bigoplus_\lambda^{0} S_\lambda\right)
 =\begin{cases}
   \mathsf{V}(B_2(G)),&\text{if some factor is not Clifford},\\
   \mathsf{V}(\flat(G)),&\text{if every factor is Clifford}.
  \end{cases}
\]
Consequently:
\begin{enumerate}[$(\rm i)$]
\item If some factor is not Clifford, $\mathcal W$ is
finitely based exactly when every factor is combinatorial.
Every negative case has no bounded-variable identity basis.
\item If every factor is Clifford, $\mathcal W$ is
finitely based exactly when $G$ has finite exponent and
has a finite basis for its group quasi-equational theory.
If $G$ has no finite exponent, $\mathcal W$ has no
bounded-variable identity basis.
\end{enumerate}
The finite-exponent condition means that all maximal subgroups
throughout the entire family share a common finite exponent.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:local-clifford-representation} to
each factor, and take the join of its Brandt-factor varieties.
The arbitrary orthogonal-sum formula in
Theorem~\ref{thm:orthogonal} combines these factors into
the stated Brandt or flat-group variety.
A class with at least two idempotents occurs precisely when
one of the original factors is not Clifford.
The orthogonal sum of the original factors embeds on the
coordinate axes of their direct product, while each factor
embeds in that sum.  It therefore generates the same join.
The preprocessing without a zero uses the identity-preserving
zero-adjunction argument already used above.

For (i), $G$ is trivial precisely when every maximal
subgroup of every factor is trivial.  Apply the all-group
Brandt classification and its bounded-variable conclusion.
For (ii), apply Theorem~\ref{thm:flat-group-all}.
Finally a direct product of groups has exponent dividing
$r$ exactly when each factor has exponent dividing $r$.

label: thm:brandt-monoid-join
title: Theorem
head: environment
name: Brandt monoid reduction

title: Proof
body_md:
First put $A=B_2^1(G)$, and take a nonempty set $K$.
Inside $A^K$, let $J$ be the set of tuples with a
zero coordinate, put
$C=(B_2(G)\setminus\{0\})^K$, and let $u$ be
the tuple of global identities.  The set
$R=J\cup C\cup\{u\}$ is a subsemiring.
Indeed $J$ absorbs both operations; products and sums
of two members of $C$ belong to $C\cup J$.
For $c\in C$, the sum $u+c$ equals $c$ if
all coordinates of $c$ are matrix idempotents, and
otherwise belongs to $J$.
Collapsing $J$ gives
\[
 R/J\cong B_{\{1,2\}^K}^1(G^K).
\]
The identification collects the left indices, group
labels, and right indices of a tuple, and sends $u$
to the global identity.  In particular it preserves
the natural meet with that identity.
Choose nonempty $K$ with $I\hookrightarrow\{1,2\}^K$
and use the diagonal embedding $G\hookrightarrow G^K$.
This embeds $B_I^1(G)$ in the quotient above.
The reverse variety inclusion follows by selecting two
indices of $I$, proving index independence.

For the remaining equality, inside $B_2^1\times
\flat(G)$ let $J$ again consist of elements
with a zero coordinate, and put
\[
 R=J\cup\{(e_{ij},g):i,j\in\{1,2\},\ g\in G\}
       \cup\{(1,1_G)\}.
\]
The same closure argument applies.  Specifically,
$(1,1_G)+(e_{ij},g)$ stays nonzero modulo $J$
exactly when $i=j$ and $g=1_G$.
Thus $R/J\cong B_2^1(G)$.
Conversely $B_2^1$ embeds using identity group labels,
and $\flat(G)$ embeds as a diagonal corner with
zero.  This proves the join formula.
All subsemirings and quotients preserve zero.
head: environment

label: cor:brandt-monoid-fb
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:brandt-monoid-fb}
If $H$ is a finite
group and $|I|\geq2$, then $B_I^1(H)$ is
nonfinitely based, including infinite index sets.
More generally the same conclusion holds for $B_I^1(G)$
whenever there are group embeddings
$H\leq G\leq H^K$ for a finite group $H$ and
a nonempty set $K$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The finite semiring $B_2^1(H)$ contains
$\{1,e_{12},0\}\cong S_7$, and is nonfinitely based
by Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-snfb}.
For the more general assertion the zero-smash lemma
and a diagonal embedding give
$\mathsf{V}(\flat(H^K))=\mathsf{V}(\flat(H))$.
The group embeddings therefore imply
$\mathsf{V}(\flat(G))=\mathsf{V}(\flat(H))$.
Equation~\eqref{eq:brandt-monoid-join} yields
$\mathsf{V}(B_I^1(G))=\mathsf{V}(B_2^1(H))$, so the identical
finite-basis status follows.

title: Corollary

set $I$ with $|I|\geq2$, the natural inverse

name: Brandt monoids of finite exponent

title: Proof
body_md:

label: prop:s7-infinite-boundary
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:s7-infinite-boundary}
There is a countably infinite, locally finite, finitely
based ai-semiring $A$ containing $S_7$ as a
subsemiring.  Its generated variety is locally finite.
head: environment
name: An infinite finitely based extension

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal U$ be defined by the ai-semiring axioms and
\[
 xy\approx yx,\qquad x^2\approx x^3.
\]
It is finitely based and contains $S_7$.
On $k$ generators, every multiplicative word reduces
to a commutative monomial with each exponent in
$\{0,1,2\}$; there are at most $3^k-1$ nonempty
such monomials.  Distributivity and idempotent addition
then leave only finitely many sums.  Thus $\mathcal U$
is locally finite.
Its countably generated free algebra $F$ is countably
infinite and generates $\mathcal U$; distinct free
generators are separated in a two-element semilattice
with the operation duplicated, which belongs to $\mathcal U$.
Put $A=F\times S_7$.  It still generates $\mathcal U$.
For any free generator $x$, the element $t=x^2$
satisfies $t^2=t$, and $s\mapsto(t,s)$ embeds
$S_7$ into $A$.
For the named-zero signature, add the three absorption
laws to $\mathcal U$ and use $s\mapsto(0_F,s)$.
The same normal form and argument apply.
head: environment

label: lem:partial-injection-finite-trace
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:partial-injection-finite-trace}
Every identity failing in an algebra of partial injections
under composition and intersection already fails in the
full symmetric inverse semiring on a finite set.
This also holds with the empty map named as zero.
head: environment
name: Finite traces

title: Proof
body_md:
Orient a failed identity as $\mathbf{p}\approx\mathbf{q}$ and choose a
pair $(a,b)$ in the value of $\mathbf{p}$ but not that of $\mathbf{q}$.
Distributivity expands each constant-free term into a
nonempty intersection of multiplicative words.
For every word occurring in $\mathbf{p}$, retain its path from
$a$ to $b$ under the given assignment.
Let $Y$ be the finite set of all vertices on these
finitely many finite paths.
Restrict every assigned partial injection to
$Y\times Y$.
All the selected paths remain, so $(a,b)$ still
belongs to the value of $\mathbf{p}$.
Composition and intersection are monotone under
restriction of the assigned relations.
The new value of $\mathbf{q}$ is therefore contained in its
old value and still omits $(a,b)$.
This is a failed evaluation in the symmetric inverse
semiring on $Y$.
If zero is named, any term containing it is the empty
map.  Such a term cannot be the chosen side $\mathbf{p}$;
if it is $\mathbf{q}$, the same argument applies.
head: environment

label: prop:infinite-natural-fb-counterexample
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:infinite-natural-fb-counterexample}
Let $T$ be the semiring of all partial bijections of
$\mathbb N$ having finite domain, with composition
and intersection.  Both $T$ and
\[
 T^1=T\cup\{\operatorname{id}_{\mathbb N}\}
\]
are countably infinite, locally finite natural inverse
semirings whose multiplicative semigroups are periodic
and not locally Clifford.  Both generate
$\mathcal R_{\cap}$, and hence have the explicit finite
basis above.  They contain $B_2^1$ and $S_7$.
All assertions hold in both stated signatures.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Finite partial bijections are closed under composition,
inversion and intersection.  Adjoining the full identity
preserves these properties.
The natural order is restriction, whose meet is intersection.
The sets are countably infinite.
For finitely many elements of $T$, the union $Y$ of
their domains and ranges is finite; they generate a
subsemiring of the finite symmetric inverse semiring
on $Y$.
For $T^1$, the generated subsemiring is contained in
that finite semiring together with the full identity.
Thus both algebras are locally finite, and in particular
every multiplicative cyclic subsemigroup is finite.

On a fixed two-point subset, take its identity, the four
singleton partial bijections, and the empty map.
They form $B_2^1$.  Its identity $e$, one off-diagonal
arrow $a$, and zero form $S_7$.
The arrow lies in $eTe$ and has distinct domain and
range idempotents, proving failure of local Cliffordness.

Every finite symmetric inverse semiring embeds in $T$.
The finite-trace lemma and the representation theorem
therefore give $\mathsf{V}(T)=\mathcal R_{\cap}$.
Since $T\subseteq T^1$ and $T^1\in\mathcal R_{\cap}$,
the latter has the same variety.
For the named-zero signature, add the three absorption
laws to the displayed finite basis.
To justify this directly, represent a model of those laws
as partial injections.  Its zero is an idempotent map,
thus the identity on some set $D$, and is contained
in every represented map.  All maps fix $D$, and
injectivity prevents points outside $D$ from mapping
into $D$.
Restricting to the complement of $D$ preserves both
operations and injectivity of the representation, and
sends zero to the empty map.
The finite-trace argument then applies unchanged.
head: environment

label: prop:infinite-clifford-sylow-boundary
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:infinite-clifford-sylow-boundary}
There is a countably infinite locally finite group $G$
of exponent $3$ such that $\flat(G)$ is finitely
based and generates a locally finite variety, although
$G$ contains a nonabelian finite $3$-group.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\mathcal N$ be the group variety defined by
\[
 x^3\approx1,\qquad [[x,y],z]\approx1,
\]
where $[x,y]=x^{-1}y^{-1}xy$.
It is locally finite by an explicit collecting argument:
in a group generated by $g_1,\ldots,g_d$, centrality
of commutators puts every element in the form
\[
 g_1^{a_1}\cdots g_d^{a_d}
 \prod_{i<j}[g_i,g_j]^{b_{ij}},
 \qquad a_i,b_{ij}\in\{0,1,2\}.
\]
There are at most $3^{d+\binom d2}$ such forms.

Let $H_1,H_2,\ldots$ represent the isomorphism types of
finite groups in $\mathcal N$, and set
\[
 G=\bigoplus_{i\geq1}H_i,
\]
the restricted direct product with finite coordinate
support.  This is a countably infinite member of
$\mathcal N$, is locally finite, and contains every
finite group in $\mathcal N$, up to isomorphism, as a
coordinate subgroup.
Every quasi-identity failing in a group of $\mathcal N$
fails on a finitely generated, hence finite, subgroup.
That subgroup embeds in $G$.
Consequently the quasi-identities of $G$ are exactly
those of $\mathcal N$.
They have the displayed finite basis relative to groups.
The finite-exponent correspondence
\cite[Lemma 2.2]{RJZL} proves that $\flat(G)$
is finitely based.

Its generated semiring variety is also
locally finite directly.
A multiplicative word on $d$ variables is determined,
as a word function on $\flat(G)$, by its variable
content and its value in the relatively free group of
$\mathcal N$ on those variables.
The collecting bound makes the number of these functions
finite.  Every semiring term is an idempotent sum of them,
so there are only finitely many term functions in each
fixed finite number of variables.

Finally $H=\operatorname{UT}_3(\mathbb F_3)$ is a
nonabelian group of order $27$, of class two and
exponent three: $(I+N)^3=I$ for every strictly upper
triangular $3$-by-$3$ matrix $N$.
Thus $H$ embeds in $G$, and $\flat(H)$ is a
subsemiring of $\flat(G)$.
The finite criterion \eqref{eq:group-criterion} makes
$\flat(H)$ nonfinitely based.
The construction and Lemma~\ref{lem:constant} also give
the named-zero assertion.
head: environment

label: thm:finite-natural-generator-replacement
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:finite-natural-generator-replacement}
Let $S$ be a natural inverse semiring.
If $\mathsf{V}(S)=\mathsf{V}(B)$ for some finite ai-semiring $B$,
there is a finite natural inverse semiring
$A$, embedded in a finite direct power of $S$, such
that $\mathsf{V}(A)=\mathsf{V}(S)$.
In particular, if such an $S$ is not locally Clifford,
it is nonfinitely based and has no bounded-variable
identity basis.  These assertions hold in both signatures.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The trivial variety is immediate, so assume it is nontrivial.
Since $B\in\mathsf{V}(S)$, choose a subsemiring $D\leq S^I$
and an onto homomorphism $q:D\to B$.
Choose one preimage for each element of $B$, and let
$R$ be their generated subsemiring in $D$.
The variety of the finite algebra $B$ is locally finite,
so $R$ is finite and $q|_R$ is still onto.
Inside $S^I$, let $A_0$ be generated by
$R\cup\{r^{-1}:r\in R\}$.
It is finite for the same local-finiteness reason.
Inversion reverses products and preserves natural meets,
so induction on terms shows that $A_0$ is inverse-closed.
It is also meet-closed, and its natural order is the
restriction of the ambient natural order.
Thus $A_0$ is a finite natural inverse semiring.

Since $R\leq A_0$ and $q|_R:R\to B$ is onto,
$B\in\mathsf{V}(A_0)$.  Hence
\[
 \mathsf{V}(B)\subseteq\mathsf{V}(A_0)\subseteq\mathsf{V}(S)=\mathsf{V}(B).
\]
Finitely many coordinates separate the finitely many
distinct pairs of elements of $A_0$.
Projection onto those coordinates is an embedding and
gives the required finite-power copy $A$.

If $S$ is not locally Clifford, choose an idempotent
$e$ and $a\in eSe$ with $d(a)\ne r(a)$.
The subsemiring generated by $e,a,a^{-1}$ is finite,
and the inverses of all its generators are present.
Since inversion reverses products and preserves natural
meets, induction on terms makes it inverse-closed.
It is still not locally Clifford.
Lemma~\ref{lem:brandt-monoid-divisor} puts $B_2^1$,
and hence $S_7$, in its generated variety.
Therefore $S_7\in\mathsf{V}(S)=\mathsf{V}(B)$.
Lemma~\ref{lem:s7-snfb} makes $B$, and hence $S$,
nonfinitely based.
Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-finite-rank} excludes a
bounded-variable basis.
In the named-zero language all generated subsemirings
and maps above preserve the designated zero.
head: environment

label: thm:finite-variety-natural-classification
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:finite-variety-natural-classification}
Let $S$ be a natural inverse semiring such that
$\mathsf{V}(S)=\mathsf{V}(B)$ for some finite ai-semiring $B$.
Then $S$ is finitely based if and only if it is locally
Clifford and at least one of the following holds:
\begin{enumerate}[$(\rm i)$]
\item $S$ is combinatorial;
\item $S$ is Clifford, and every finite $p$-subgroup
of every maximal subgroup of $S$ is abelian, for every
prime $p$.
\end{enumerate}
Every nonfinitely based case has no bounded-variable identity
basis.  The criterion holds in both signatures, without a
cardinality restriction on $S$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-natural-generator-replacement},
there are a finite natural inverse semiring $A$ and an
embedding $A\leq S^n$, for some finite $n$, such that
$\mathsf{V}(A)=\mathsf{V}(S)$.  Finite basability is therefore the same
for $A$ and $S$.

We first compare their structural properties.
Local Cliffordness is equivalent to
\eqref{eq:regular-flat-identity} in the natural inverse
class, by Theorem~\ref{thm:regular-flat-identity}.
Since $A,S$ have the same identities, one is locally
Clifford exactly when the other is.
Cliffordness and being combinatorial pass from $S$ to
the inverse subsemigroup $A\leq S^n$: domain and range
idempotents agree coordinatewise in the Clifford case,
and all coordinate images of a subgroup are trivial in
the combinatorial case.
They also pass from $A$ to $S$, using the finiteness
of $A$.
If $A$ is Clifford, a common finite exponent $r$ of
its maximal subgroups gives the identity
$x^{r+1}\approx x$.  It holds in $S$, forcing every
element of $S$ to lie in a cyclic subgroup.
If $A$ is combinatorial, its finite multiplicative
semigroup satisfies $x^{m+1}\approx x^m$ for some
$m\geq1$.  This identity holds in $S$ and excludes
every nontrivial subgroup.  Thus each of the three
structural properties agrees for $A$ and $S$.

Suppose first that $S$ satisfies the proposed criterion.
If it is combinatorial, so is $A$; the finite
classification makes $A$, and hence $S$, finitely
based.
Otherwise $S$ and $A$ are Clifford.
Let $P$ be a Sylow subgroup of any maximal subgroup of
$A$.  It is a finite $p$-group for some prime $p$.
Each coordinate projection of the embedding $A\leq S^n$
maps $P$ to a finite $p$-subgroup of a maximal
subgroup of $S$.  These images are abelian by hypothesis.
The projections jointly separate elements, so any two
elements of $P$ commute.  All the required Sylow
subgroups of $A$ are abelian, and the finite
classification again gives finite basability.

Conversely suppose $S$, and therefore $A$, is finitely
based.  The finite classification makes $A$ locally
Clifford, so $S$ is locally Clifford as well.
If $A$ is combinatorial, the structural comparison
already proves (i).
Otherwise $A$, and hence $S$, is Clifford.
Suppose a maximal subgroup $G_e$ of $S$ had a finite
nonabelian $p$-subgroup $P$.
The flat-group projection of
Theorem~\ref{thm:clifford-natural} gives
\[
 \flat(P)\in\mathsf{V}(\flat(G_e))
 \subseteq\mathsf{V}(S)=\mathsf{V}(A).
\]
If $S$ has no zero, first use the identity-preserving
binary-language zero adjunction of
Remark~\ref{rem:clifford-nozero}.
The finite-target theorem
\cite[Theorem 6.1]{JRZ}, already used in
Theorem~\ref{thm:three-obstructions}, now makes the finite
ai-semiring $A$ nonfinitely based: its variety contains
the finite semiring $\flat(P)$, which has a
nonabelian nilpotent subgroup.
This contradicts the choice of $A$.  Thus (ii) holds.

Finally $\mathsf{V}(S)=\mathsf{V}(B)$ is locally finite because $B$
is finite and the signature is finite.
Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-finite-rank} therefore excludes a
bounded-variable identity basis in every negative case.

label: rem:finite-variety-group-period
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:finite-variety-group-period}
Under the hypothesis of
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-variety-natural-classification},
every maximal subgroup of $S$ is locally finite, and
these groups have a common finite exponent.
For the first assertion, a finite set of group generators
together with their inverses generates a finite subsemiring,
by local finiteness of $\mathsf{V}(B)$; the generated group is
contained in that finite subsemiring.
For the second, the finite multiplicative semigroup of
$B$ satisfies $x^{m+r}\approx x^m$ for some
$m,r\geq1$.  The same identity holds in $S$.
Inside any subgroup it cancels to $g^r=1$.
The classification applies when $\mathsf{V}(S)$ has a finite
generating algebra.

label: prop:not-inherent
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:not-inherent}
Every finite regular flat semiring, and every finite
natural Clifford semiring, belongs to a locally
finite finitely based variety of ai-semirings.  Therefore
none is inherently nonfinitely based, in either stated
language.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $S$ be nonzero.  In the regular flat case use
its decomposition and finite product group $G$.
In the natural Clifford case use the finite product group
in Theorem~\ref{thm:clifford-natural}.
The exact variety formulas and the group-corner inclusion
give $S\in\mathsf{V}(B_2(G))$ in both cases.
Thus its multiplicative reduct
belongs to the semigroup variety of the finite
multiplicative semigroup $T=B_2(G)$.
The latter has a finite identity basis $\Delta$, by
\cite[Corollary 2]{Volkov19}; that result includes the
finite-group case using the finite group basis theorem.
For the trivial group one may use the usual three
Brandt semigroup identities.

Add $\Delta$ to the finite ai-semiring axioms and call
the resulting variety $\mathcal U$.  It contains $S$
and is finitely based.  It is also locally finite.
Indeed, the semigroup variety generated by finite $T$
is locally finite: on $k$ generators its free elements
are term functions on the finite set $T^k$, of which
there are finitely many.  Fix representatives of these
word classes.  Distributivity expands every semiring term
in $k$ variables into a sum of words, and $\Delta$
reduces each word to one of the fixed representatives.
Commutative idempotent addition leaves finitely many
possible sums.  Thus the free $k$-generated semiring
in $\mathcal U$ is finite.

In the named-zero language add the three absorption laws;
terms containing zero give one additional normal form.
The same local finiteness proof applies.  The zero-only
algebra has a trivial envelope separately.

label: lem:brandt-zimin-minimal
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $c=e_{12}$, $d=e_{21}$, and suppose
\[
 B_2^1\models \mathbf{u}+Z_n\approx Z_n.
\]
Equivalently $Z_n\leq_{\rm nat}\mathbf{u}$ under every assignment.
An extra variable in $\mathbf{u}$ is impossible: assign it
zero and all other variables the identity, obtaining
the false inequality $1\leq_{\rm nat}0$.
Thus $\mathbf{u}$ uses only $x_1,\ldots,x_n$.

For each $i$, assign
\[
 x_j\longmapsto
 \begin{cases}
 1,&j<i,\\
 c,&j=i,\\
 d,&j>i.
 \end{cases}
\]
The recursion and $cdc=c$ give value $c$ for
$Z_n$.
The off-diagonal matrix unit $c$ is maximal in the
natural order and is incomparable with $1$;
therefore $\mathbf{u}$ also has value $c$.

Let $\mathbf{u}_i$ be the word obtained from $\mathbf{u}$ by deleting
all letters of index less than $i$, with the auxiliary
convention $\mathbf{u}_{n+1}=\varepsilon$.
Under this assignment its $x_i$'s read as $c$ and
its larger letters as $d$.
The relations $c^2=d^2=0$ force any nonzero such
word to alternate.
An alternating word has value $c$ exactly when it
begins and ends with $c$; even lengths give $cd$
or $dc$, and odd lengths beginning with $d$ give
$d$.
Consequently
\[
 \mathbf{u}_i=x_i y_1x_i y_2x_i\cdots y_qx_i,\qquad
 \mathbf{u}_{i+1}=y_1\cdots y_q,
\]
where $q\geq0$ and each $y_j$ has index greater than $i$.
For $i=n$ this gives $\mathbf{u}_n=x_n$.
Descending induction then reconstructs each $\mathbf{u}_i$
uniquely by inserting $x_i$ before, between, and
after the letters of $\mathbf{u}_{i+1}$.
These are exactly the successive projections of
$Z_n$.  Hence $\mathbf{u}=\mathbf{u}_1=Z_n$ literally.

label: cor:brandt-monoid-inherent
title: Corollary
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In the binary language apply the quoted criterion to
Lemma~\ref{lem:brandt-zimin-minimal}.
For the named-zero language, a valid identity of
$B_2^1$ either contains no zero constant or contains
zero on both sides.
Indeed any term containing zero is identically zero,
whereas a constant-free term takes value $1$ when
all variables are $1$.
Name the existing absorbing zero of each $T_k$.
It now satisfies all at-most-$k$-variable identities
of the expansion, including those with zero.
If a locally finite finitely based variety contained
that expansion, choose $k$ bounding its finite basis.
Then it would contain the infinite finitely generated
$T_k$, a contradiction.

label: thm:finite-natural-inherent
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:finite-natural-inherent}
For a finite natural inverse semiring $S$,
in either stated signature,
\[
 S\text{ is inherently nonfinitely based}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S\text{ is not locally Clifford}.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $S$ is locally Clifford, its finite regular flat
orthogonalization has the same identities by
Theorem~\ref{thm:local-clifford-representation}.
Proposition~\ref{prop:not-inherent} puts that
orthogonalization, and hence $S$, in a locally finite
finitely based variety.  The zero-only case has a trivial
envelope as well.
If $S$ is not locally Clifford, the semiring divisor
lemma gives $B_2^1\in\mathsf{V}(S)$.
By Corollary~\ref{cor:brandt-monoid-inherent}, no locally
finite finitely based variety can contain $S$, since
it would then contain $B_2^1$.
This is precisely the required INFB assertion; finiteness
ensures that $\mathsf{V}(S)$ itself is locally finite.
head: environment

label: cor:locally-finite-variety-nonlocal
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:locally-finite-variety-nonlocal}
Let $S$ be a natural inverse semiring with
$\mathsf{V}(S)$ locally finite.  If $S$ is not locally
Clifford, it is inherently nonfinitely based and has no
bounded-variable identity basis.
If, more specifically, $\mathsf{V}(S)=\mathsf{V}(B)$ for some finite
algebra $B$, then
\[
 S\text{ is inherently nonfinitely based}
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 S\text{ is not locally Clifford}.
\]
There is no cardinality restriction on $S$.
Both assertions hold in both signatures.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
In the nonlocal case choose an idempotent $e$ and
$a\in eSe$ with $d(a)\ne r(a)$.
The subsemiring $N=\langle e,a,a^{-1}\rangle$ is finite
by local finiteness of $\mathsf{V}(S)$.
The inverses of its generators are present, inversion
reverses products, and inversion preserves natural meets.
Induction on terms therefore makes $N$ inverse-closed.
It remains non-locally-Clifford, so the finite divisor
lemma gives $B_2^1\in\mathsf{V}(N)\subseteq\mathsf{V}(S)$.
No locally finite finitely based variety containing $S$
can then exist, by Corollary~\ref{cor:brandt-monoid-inherent}.
The bounded-variable assertion follows from
Lemma~\ref{lem:locally-finite-rank}.

Under the finite-generator hypothesis, take the finite
natural inverse replacement $A\leq S^n$ from
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-natural-generator-replacement}.
If $S$ is locally Clifford, so is this inverse
subsemigroup $A$ of its direct power.
Theorem~\ref{thm:finite-natural-inherent} puts $A$
in a locally finite finitely based variety.
Since $\mathsf{V}(A)=\mathsf{V}(S)$, the same variety contains $S$.
This proves the reverse direction.
